THE DOUBLE-SHIF SYSTFIL

THE objections so ably urged by Mr. LLOYD
Jos in the BEE-HIVE, of Sept. 28th, are
'worthy of that serious attention which every-
thing which he utters on questions affecting
working men must always command. And I
am sorry that accident alone has prevented I/19
from taking an earlier notice of his vigorous
criticism. I think I can satisfy him.

Let mo begin by saying that I do not make
myself the apostle of the new proposal. I ilud
it thrown out as a practical suggestion by a
groat employer, and all that I recommend is
that it should be fairly considered and tried.
It rests neither with me nor with the workmen
to introduce it in practice. There is nothing
immediate before us. The plan can only be
introduced by the employers themselves. All
I say is, that if it were ever offered to them, I
think the workmen would be wise to look on
it with favour.

Now, as I have said before, reasoning on the
indirect consequences of any new step in
economic progress is always extremely
hazardous. The complexity of these social
laws is such that it is hardly possible to predict
any but the most direct results from any given
fact. The farmers insisted that Free Trade
must ruin them. The paper-makers vowed
that the French Treaty would be their death.
And it was not very easy to show a priori
that their fears were unreasonable. The world,
however, saw too many immediate advan-
tages in Free Trade and in the late treaty to be
stopped by these possible dangers. And in the
result neither the farmers nor the paper.
makers were extinguished. It is, therefore, I
think, a very good rule never to sacrifice a
.present direct eoonomic advantage under a
vague apprehension of distant and indirect
consequences, which may turn out in fifty
different ways. If the men. see their way to a
rise in wages, they do not give too great weight
to theoretic prophecies that it will ruin the
trade. And so, if they had the eight hours'
day offered to them, I do not think they would
refuse it, on the ground of its possible operation
on the state of population. In all economic
questions we cannot be too much on our guard
against logical consequences. They are in-
finitely difficult to trace out, and elude us like
a will-o'-the-wisp.
Now I think Mr. LLOYD JONES'S argument
is based upon one of these logical quicksands.
The proposal of Mr. BHASSEY was this—to
substitute for the ten hours day a sixteen hours
day, worked by two shifts of men at eight
hours each. The argument of Mr. LLOYD
JONES is based on the assumption that this
implies the doubling of the number of workers,
and, the increase of production 60 per cent.

Now the assumption is unsound. The double
-
shift system might conceivably be introduced
without any increase either in the numbers of
the workmen or the amount of production.

Not only is this perfectly possible, but it is
possible in two different ways. Exactly the
same number of men might be employed in
fewer "works" by a less number of em-
ployers; or, on the other hand, the "works"
might be reduced. in extent, have smaller
capital, machinery, and plant, and employ
fewer men at the same moment. Now the

atter of these suggestions, though perfectly

possible, is not very probable. But the
former is not only possible, but, to a certain

degree, most probable. Let us take a prac-
tical example from the London building trade.
_ _ .

Hero about one-third, or nearly half, the
workmen are employed by the groat firms with
a costly plant and a regular staff. The rest
are employed by small contractors with a much
smaller apparatus, and on rather irregular
terms. Many of them are more jobbers,
middlemen, and the like, who spring up and
disappear as " masters " altogether suddenly.
Now any great firm introducing the double-
shift system would absorb the workmen and
, the business of many of these casual em-
ployers, and even find room for them on their
own staff. The offer of" the eight hour day"
would naturally draw off the workmen from
the firms which worked ten. The building
trade of the metropolis would be concentrated,
and instead of being subdivided amongst
hundreds of small contractors, it would fall

more generally to the larger. If the small con-
tractors complain, I would not tell them " to
take care of themselves," as is too often said to
workmen when suddenly dismissed. If the
change was not violent, all this would easily
be adjusted; and it is only what occurs in the
constant fluctuations of the trade. Our times
are not favourable to the increase of the
smaller employers, and I think the future may
be less so. I have always understood that
workmen and their sooieties prefer to deal with

the great firms, having a large business,
regular conditions, and great responsibility ;
and I imagine the workmen would have no
reason to complain if such firms verylargely
absorbed the business and workmen of most of
the less established and less responsible con-
tractors.

Here, therefore, we have an assumption per-
fectly possible, and even natural, under which
the double-shift system would involve no in-
crease whatever in the number of the work-
men, and not only no increase in production,
but, in fact, a diminution. Tile only great
change would be a great reduction in the num-
ber of employers. This is, of course, an
extreme assumption, but it is a perfectly legi-
timate one. And I use it only to show that
the double-shift system is not the same thing
necessarily as the increase of the workmen 100
per cent. and of production 60 per cent. So
that all objections based on the assumption
that the one follows from the other falls to the
ground.
But though it would be perfectly possible
to work the double-shift without increasing
the workers on the production, I am far from
saying that this is the probable result. What
we have is an immense latitude from that
point up to the other extreme of doubling the
numbers and increasing production 60 per
cent., every one of the intermediate stops being
, perfectly possible and natural. Here and there
' it would happen that more workmen were

attracted to the trade; here and there business

would be concentrated, and fewer firms would

exist; here and there firms might do the busi-
ness with less plant. All these possibilities
would form an infinite sot of combinations
under the necessities of business and by those
wonderful laws which industry accommodates

itself to changed conditions. What the double-
shift would give us would be an instrument of
extraordinary range, by means of which, as
the need might arise, the numbers of the
workmen might be largely increased, whilst
the amount of production might be slightly
increased, and the number of the capitalists
might be reduced, all of these adapting
themselves to the occasion required. The
extreme limit of increasing the workmen
100 per cent. and. the production 60 per
cent. would never, I think, be reached in
practice, and we are not in the least bound to
provide against its possible dangers.
At the same time, though, I think the general
introduction of the" shift" would never lead to
this hypothetical increase. I think it would.
very probably lead to a considerable increase
in the number of the workmen, and a certain
increase in the amount of production. The
two, it will be seen, are not in the same ratio.
For unless the work of eight hours could be
made as productive as that of ten hours, it
would' require more than 20 per cent. more
workmen to maintain the same amount of pro-
duction; and 50 per cent. more workmen
would involve only 20 per cent. increased pro-
duction. A considerable increase in the
number of the workmen, however, is what I
should certainly expect. And I have not the
least doubt that there is an ample reserve of

them. I thought the immense unemployed
surplus was an acknowledged fact. Every
reduction of the hours of labour implies such
a reserve, unless it is to have the effect of
diminishing production. It has, indeed, been
a very popular argument, that the object of
reducing the hours of labour is to find work
for this unemployed reserve. Without
endorsing this argument,!we may be sure the
reserve is there. My suggestion, in fact, does
not imply a sudden doubling of the workmen
employed. As a matter of fact, their numbers
are rapidly and constantly being increased.
Production is not a fixed limit. It is rapidly
advancing, and we cannot check it. What
the "double-shift" might do is to enable this
increase to take place in one way rather than
another, in a way that promises economic
advantages and shorter hours rather than in a
way that does not. I therefore abstain from
entering on any of the arguments drawn from
a supposed doubling of the population, or the
vast evils of over-production, because I cannot
see any connection between the double-shift
system and either of these dangers.
As Mr. BILAStiEr has shown us, the trade of
the kingdom has actually doubled in fifteen
years. There is, therefore, an enormous power
of expansion in our industry, and a constant
demand for fresh workmen. How, I ask, have
these been provided for hitherto? And what
grounds have we for thinking that the same
facts will not continue? Again, let us note
the vast difference between the numbers em-
ployed when trade is very dull and. when it is
very brisk. There are times, perhaps, when in
particular trades not half the workmen are
employed, and, again, others in which in brief
periods double the number of those employed.
It is a very complex and difficult question to
answer—how is that surplus maintained awl

whence does the increase come ? They do,
however, in spite of bad times, and they are
found, when wanted, in good times. And all
this proves to us the incredible elasticity of
the labour market, a state of things full of
evil, no doubt. But I fail to see how any

of those evils would be inoreased if the men

----
were regularly a work on the double-shift

plan, as coal-miners, railway and ship en-
gineers, and many other workmen already are.
It is not my intention to follow Mr. LLOYD
JONES at any length into several minor diffi-
culties lie suggests, because I do not admit
his original objection that the plan involves
doubling the workmen. As I conceive the
double-shift system, it would involve the re-
organizations of industry, rather than its
sudden expansion. No one ever dreamed of
introducing it by Act of Parliament, or any
artificial stimulus. It would come about
simply under the impulse of supply and
demand, and the total production of the
country would bear the same relation to the
demand for its products as it does now. The
questions of "short time," and" depression of
trade," would remain just where they do
now. Men would not be employed under the
relay system or any other system, unless there
was a market for their labour. In the rare
cases in which it is necessary for a trade to
work half-time, nothing would be easier.
The " day " would be reduced to eight
hours for the works, and the relays would
each work half-time, or else the works would
run only three days a week. But why is such
a disaster to be more dreaded under the relay
system than under any other system?
If any firm adopted this system, it would
only be because they had a capital and a
market equal to support it. The whole argu-
ment, in fact, turns on this. Since no
artificial aid to the relay system is suggested,
its introduction is only possible under a legi-
timate economic demand. It is, therefore, not
disposed of by objections which suppose it
introduced without that economic demand.
The economic demand for better utilizing ma.
chine!, stares us in the face. The eeonornie
(and social) demand for shorter hours stares
us in the face. All I ask is, how are these two
to be made compatible unless by the relay
system?
One or two of the objections raised are, I
confess, a little strained. The notion that the
relay system will lead to a working day of six.
teen hours strikes me as rather humorous.
What power on earth is going to induce our
engineers and masons to work sixteen hours
against their will ? One example is
enough. Has the relay system had the
smallest tendency to do this in coal mines?
Precisely the contrary. It is, then, the great
protection against long hours. As to the objec-
tion that the system would destroy the
engineering trade, it must not be forgotten
that the great bulk of that trade is absorbed
by export, by the alteration and by the re-
placing of worn-out machinery. But a per-
centage of our machinery trade goes to furnish
the plant of the new growth of our own trade.
And it must not be forgotten, again, that
machinery running continuously sixteen hours
would wear out more rapidly than machinery

But I principally rely on results. In.the
coal trade, in ships, and railways, the relay
system has been largely employed, and always
with good results. The millers, I believe,
have for some time bean. agitating for its in-
troduction into the °sand coal4ol4s. In the
coal trade it has brought shorter hours, and
better conditions in all. respects. It is not
then attended with any of the terrible results
which are now threatened us. For my part, I
look on the relay system as a thing whieb is
certain to come in some day, but which had
better come gradually and tentatively. It is
to my mind the true economic supply of an
economic want. And if it be introduced wisely
and naturally, under the pressure of an econo-
mic demand, I see no connection that it can
have with over-population, over-production, or
stagnation of txade.

Tinto are points in ,Idord Dula's- Preston
•spbeeh wbioh cannot be dismissed in a few
words, awl which it would be altogether wron
to past over in silence. Our influential noble-
men and great statesmen are worth attending
to when they undertake to handle public ques-
tions. It is their duty, nay, their business,
to understand them. If providence has given
them the faculty to comprehend and explain.
there is profit in listening to them. If they
have not this faculty—if their thonght is
faulty, and ;their speech foolish,—even then
it is useful to listen, as by so doing we learn
how absurd it is to trust the conduct of pub,,
lie affairs to men, on the supposition that thy
possess 51. special fitness which only stupidity
and prejudice would expect to find.

Lord- DERUY'R utterances are regarded as
amongst the best of their kind. In his utter-
anew; we are enoouragedto expeot a coolness and
soundness like that which belongs to well-
bottled and carefully calmed old port of a
good vintage. With this Preston speech, how-
ever, as with moat that he utters, we have
been disappointed. It iS not only full of doubts
and hesitations, as we last week stated, but it
hats one or two points which would deserve to be
very harshly characterised were it not that the
cause of the people, having reason and justice
to ,Prest on, almost necessarily demands calm
and temperate advocacy.
• It is easy to seethat the Earl of DERBY,
though he airs himself in a garb of
humility and modesty, has a very high
notion 61 his dignity as a Peer and of
his rights as a landlord. But, while he
is disposed to do what is necessary to uphold
this dignity and his right, he is quite willing
and most anxious that others should take On
themselves the toil and the expense of labour-
ing for the improvement of the masses of the
people. Ile wants a now Doomsday book, that
titles to estates should be made valid and clear
of obstruction—a new edition of an old work,
corrected and amended, with proprietory rights
reserved and obligations omitted; owners re-
lieved from ancient responsibilities, and the
nation made to pay for their default; a settle-
ment now, in favour of possessors, which in a
little time might be made with an eye to the
rights and interests of the nation. It is a wise
spirit of prevision on the part of his lordship
which seeks to close up a settlement remaining
inconveniently open. The people of England,
however, it is to be hoped, will not permit this
settlement until they have carefully enquired
why and wherefore the many obligations im-
posed upon possessors of land by the conditions
under which they originally obtained it, have
not been fulfilled?

We postpone this very interesting subject to
notice the following,:which is about ea rich a
specimen in its way of elms arrogance as it
would be possible to imagine. After the
speaker had cast doubt on co-operation in one
of its most difficult forms—productive industry
—and referred to co-operation as applied to the
land for the improvement of the condition of
the agricultural labourer, he spoke thus—"l
don't say that it (co-operation) should not he
tried; or that in some form it may not ultimately
answer; only with our present experience, I
should advise to one to put more money into
it than he can afford conveniently to lose.
But why should not the question be praetioally

tested. ? There are plenty of estates in the
market, the trading co-operative associations
of this country are very numerous, they have
a good deal of money made, and their sup-
porters are enthusiastically zealous in the
cause. A very little experience is better than
a good deal of talk; let them try a few farms,
and see whether they can work them to ad-
vantage on their principle. If they succeed,
nobody *ill grudge them their success; if they
wenn only where we were." This ought
to be read over twice. The length, and
breadth, and depth of its assurance oannot be
understood unless the importance and meaning
of every world are thoroughly studied. The
question, it must be remembered, is the im-
proVement oi the condition of the agricultural
labourer, and the person who speaks is a pro-
minent member of that class, which, as law-
makers and landlords,have always hadtbe fate
of these poor fellows in their hands; until
recently almost everything was theirs—pro-
perty, which consisted chiefly of the land and
and its produce belonged, to them. Nothing
as legislation could be done without their con-
sent, and anything that wisdom, humanity, or
sound policy could have dictated, they might
have embodied in the law for the benefit of the
people. This, however, was not their function;
they never saw their way to making this their
duty. They lay on the land like huge sponges,
sucking up and absorbing its rich juices,
leaving to the industrious population labour,
beggary, and despair. There never was in any
period of the world's history, or under any
condition of its existence, a class which took
so muoh and gave so little in return. When
land and the produce of land was the only
wealth, they clutched at it and held it. And
now that the produce and wealth of the world
are flowing into our lap as a nation by the
ingenuity and industry of our people, it is not
to them we owe the blessing—to them, in fact,
we owe impediments to its fruition which for
years caused dearth and affliction in the
nation.

What have they done as a class to make
tugland what she is? What fructifying in-
vention do we owe to them? What commer-
cial explorations for the widening of our
markets ? what enterprise in the extension, ac-
cumulation, and activity of our mechanical pro-
ducing power? The sponges simply sat still and
sucked; when new towns sprung up as homes
for our busy manufacturing people, they looked
on, and raised the rent. They saw a power
growing up beside them which they were far
too elevated to touch in a friendly spirit, but
by no means too proud to plunder and grow
rich by. Bad as the influence of the new rich
class was, it was far better than what our
great nobility exercised as it put upon men
the necessity of rising together and put into
each some hope of rising.
Even in the towns the struggle for the
working man was a hard one, not so hard or
so hopeless as that of the man in the fields, but
still in all conscience:severe enough. The one
set of workers, now, by aid of co-operation,
trades unionism and other helpful agencies, are
dragging themselves slowly and painfully out
of the slough into which an ill-regulated,
selfish competition thing them prostrate ; the
other is stirring, only stirring, half-blindly
stirring, to the alarm of Earl DERBY and
others who up to this time have lived amongst
them, and witnessed their miseries without
making any noble, resolute, or general effort
for their rescue. They have been unanimous_
and active in preserving their game, but they
have not, to their shame, been unanimous or
active in preserving their men; in cherishing
the workers whose labour made them what
they are. They, by their stupid and heart-
less neglect, have brought things to the
pass in which we find them, and they can
now neither suggest nor do anything to lift up
the poor and give them comfort and hope.
Would it not be a noble act for Lord DERBY
and other lords, who have land lying about in
all directions—hid in valleys, spread out in
plains, piled up in mountains—to put them-
selves in comnumication with the millionaires
of the towns and cities, and say---,4 We have
grown great
.by the labour of the people, and
you have grown rich by their ingenuity and
industry; why cannot we give land and you
money, to set on; foot experiments from which

to inaugurate changes needed by them, and
useful to us, if for no other reason but that we
may enjoy what we possess in security? Let
us, as it were, unite beneficence and power, to
drive ignorance, poverty, and fear from the
laud."

This would be a noble league, tvorthy Our
two aristocracies—that of land and that of
money. Instead of this, what does the states-
man of Knowlsey do? He suggests that as
there are estates in the market which may be
had for money, and that as the co-operators of
the north, the prudent, struggling, self-
denying working men, have made money by
co-operation, they should try the experiment
practically, at their own expense, and "if
they succeeded, r ()body would grudge them
their success; if they failed, we are only
where we were."

Surely the force of assurance cannot go be-
yond this! They—the 'nobility and gentry—
who have beggared the people by making
profit out of them they who have enor-
mously increased their possessions and piled
up wealth whilst these poor agricultural
labourers have beeti sinking in poverty and
' misery, now turn to working men in the
towns, who are struggling to save themselves
by a grand principle—their own in discovery
and in application—and tell them they will let
them or sell them land on which to invest
their savings for experimental purposes, that
the beggars and paupers they have made, and
the hungry labourers they cannot feed, may
be rescued from the misery brought upon their'
by the frauds, impositions, and oppressions to
which they have bad to submit.
What can anybody think of such a proposal
as this? Nobles, law-makers, statesmen, the
accredited .governors [and rulers of the land;
rich, powerful, inflaentill men ; men upon
whose heads rest awful responsibilities before
GOD and man ; those to whom
.the poor cry in
their distress. These, I say, by the mouth of
Lord DERBY, ask the.a.rtizans in the towns to
'save the working men in the fields, who are
now a disgrace and a terror to. those above
them.

This is the proposal of Lord DERBY; and
this proposal is a practical abdication of
authority in the class to which he belongs. If
the redemption of the masses is to come in this
way, then it is time that Lord DERBY and his
fellows should clear out. By his confession
they are of no practical use to the nation, and,
like all other shams, the sooner they take
themselves away the bettor; or, at least, the
sooner they give up their exclusive pretensions
the bettor, in many senses, it will be for the
nation,

No doubt the co-operators of England, in
duty to their principle, as well as in the pro-
motion of their interests, will make the attempt
to establish co-operative farming. They have
a, certain market for the produce, and they
can, when the moment arrives for commencing,
carry on the work without much risk. But
they must not be challenged to this by men
like Earl DERBY, nor must their fitness for
such a work be made a reason why he and his
class should allow misery and destitution to
spread and deepen daily round the walls of
their proud ,'mansions. They have stripped
and starved the lublurer and housed him like
a hog; and instead of indulging in speech-
making, they should fling aside their robes of
State, put their coronets on the shelf for a
season, and set to work like earnest honest
men to save the country from the dangers
brought on it by their inhutuan neglects.

LLOYD JONES.

THE BALLOT ACT.

ought not to require any paid agent for the

We rejoice to see that the Labour Repro'
sentation League is stilling in this matte'
They could not take a better step for the plit"
pose of rendering the Ballot Act—what it wiel

IT is beyond all doubt that the only reason
why the first French loan for ten millions
was subscribed for and paid in gold without
exercising much or any disturbance in the
money market of this country consisted of the
fact that it was paid by the gold currency
which existed in France, for if there is one
Ailing more certain than another in monetary
affairs, it is that it is impossible for a gold
currency to circulate with an inconvertible
paper currency unlimited in amount, yet
made a legal tender.
It was a similar paper currency 'which
enabled America to carry on the civil war
which ended in victory, and which has
enabled France to pay the enormous sum
whieh Prussia demanded as the price of
yielding up the greater part of the French
provinces which she had conquered; and, it is
not a little strange, it was this very system of
paper currency whioh secured such enormous
advantages for America and for France, but
guarded against abuse by being limited in
amount, that I asked Mr. GLADSTONE to in-
quire into, with the view of preventing those
monetary panics which periodically have been
the curse of the country, for the Gazett

proves that they drive thousands of our less
affluent merchants, manufacturers, and trades-

men to bankruptcy or insolvency, and these
are the principal employers of the working
class, often limiting and sometimes preventing
them from obtaining that employment by
which alone they can procure wages to obtain
food for themselves and families.

And not only would Mr. GLIDSTON.E have
given this inestimable boon to the working
()lasses, but he would also have paid off above
one hundred millions of the National Debt,
thereby reducing above three millions of
annual taxation, enabling him to have taken
off the whole duty upon tea and coffee,
another inestimable boon to the working class;
but instead of his colleagues and himself
doing this, Mr. Lowz ,runs down and airs his
platitudes at Glasgow, boasting of that great
increase of revenue which had happened
during the time his colleagues and himself
had been in. office, but with which they had.
about as much to do as with the rising and.
setting of the sun.
He also boasted of himself and colleagues
having paid off fifteen millions of debt, but
concealed the fact that they had done this by,
adopting Mr. DISRA.ELI'S plan of granting ter-
minable annuities; and he also concealed the
fact that he had personally neglected to inquire
into a plan for paying off above a hundred
millions of the National Debt; and although
himself and colleagues, believing themselves
infallible, refused this enquiry because it in-
volved an inconvertible paper currency, yet it is
almostbeyond a doubt that they will be obliged
to adopt an inconvertible currency, and with-
out the advantage which I proposed of paying
off a hundred millions of the National Debt.
Such are our financiers!
If Mr. Lowl; had understood his duty as
Chancellor of the Exchequer, he would have
warned the citizens of Glasgow that a monetary
panic) was not far 'distant, for the French second
loan of a hundred and twenty millions had
been subscribed for, the deposit paid, and. also
the first instalment, which was due *2lst Sep-
tember; how these two payments amount to
twenty millions, and which the subscribers

would doubtleis make every exertion not to
lose. Yet how is the second instalment to be
paid, and to be paid in gold? Although a
Freneh loan there is no gold in France, and its
°latency consists of inconvertible paper cur-
rency,- unlimited in amount, yet made a legal
tender' , and, according to her official journal,
her expenditure this year exceeds income
by nearly four millions, to pay which there
must be a fresh issue of paper, infallibly de-
preciating the whole of the currency.

Where, then, is the gold to come from which
is to pay the second instalment, due the 11th
day of October P and assuming that to be paid,
there are eighteen other instalments to 'be paid

4an the llth-of each -mouth. Xruly the Israelites
have learnt something from the barbarous
treatment they received from their Norman
oppressors of extracting their teeth gradually
until the loan was obtained, and it is by such
a gradual operation alone that the ROTHS-
CIIILDS of Europe more surely attain their end.
It is certain as the sun at noonday that there
is only one country in the world which can
find sufficient gold to pay the remainder of the
instalments, and that country is England, not
, the Bank of England, but England.

For we know by the returns that the bullion
and gold coin in the ooffers of the Bank of
England is only twenty-two millions, ever:
shilling of which she has mortgaged in ,pay
notes; she has issued to the extent of above

although she well knew
pro-

when she made that promise she would not

When, therefore, she had used these twenty-

TEE 'WAGGON MAIIIII.B.

Two meetings of the operatives in this trade
have been held in Birmingham and Smethwick
during the past week for the purpose of consoli-
dating and adding numbers to their recently
formed union. Addresses were delivered by
Messrs. John Osborne, E. M. Adams, and Joseph
Morris, secretary, on Trades Unionism and its
advantages.
The speakers were well received, and a deter-
mination was arrived at to invite those gentlemen
to attend other meetings to be held in the locality
to give the absent men the benefit of their advice.

DUDLEY.
THE COLLIERY ENGINE TEETERS.

The colliery engine tenters and the Dudley. and
Great Bridge districts have given 14 days' notice
for an advance in wages to 6s. per day of eight
hours, and have intimated in plain terms their
intention to turn out on strike unless the demand
is conceded.

THE lIIONWORKERS.
On Saturday a meeting of delegates represent-
ing nearly the whole of the South Staffordshire
• Ironworkers was held at Groat Bridge, to consider
various matters of dispute as to the prevailing
systems of work. A discussion lasting two hours
ensued on the question of shortening the hours
of labour, but no practical result followed. The
substitution for the present six-heat system of one
of five heats was proposed, but denounced by the
majority as impracticable. The custom of re-
quiring 120Ib. to the cwt. from the puddlers was
condemned in strong terms and the following
resolution was carried unanimously
That a just weight principle be adopted by the
ironworkers generally, and that an endeavour be
made to establish such a principle as the means of
shortening the hours of labour.
In this case no definite action is probable before
January at least, the ironworkers of South
Staffordshire being bound until that time by the
wages agreement now in force.

- LIVERPOOL.
sTRIKB OF DOCK LAIJOURERR.

The Liverpool merchants and shipowners
having objected to bind themselves not to employ
foremen except they are connected with the Dock
Labourers' Society, about 4,000 dock labourers
have turned out on strike. On Wednesday the
men held an open-air meeting, and resolved to
appoint delegates to confer with the nristers, but
expressed themselves determined to keep out on
strike until the masters come to their terms.

SHEFFIELD.
TUE FILE TRAIJE.

A serious strike is threatened in the Sheffield
file trade. The question is one of equalisation of
payments for different kinds of files, involving in
some eases higher wages.

delegation, in connection with the short time
and advance of wages movement, was held on
Saturday night at the Brown Bear, Broad-street,
Bloomsbury, Mr. Davis, of the general union,
occupying the chair. The chairman said that
since the last meeting the strike at Corbett and
M'Clymont's, at Brompton, bad been satisfactorily
closed, and there were no disputes existing with
any other firm. Ile believed it was the general
feeling ;in the trade that no further levies were
necessary, and that the existing delegation be die.

of their memorial—viz., nine hours per day, at ed.

Mr. Cayryr then moved the following resolu-

MEETING OF JOURNEYMEN
FARRIERS.

A large meeting of the journeymen farriers,
embracing both society and non-society men, was
hold on Monday night at the Foresters' Hall,
Wilderness-row, St. Luke's, Mr. Ash in the chair,
for the purpose of receiving a report from the
amalgamated committee relative to their confer-
ence with the employers.
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said
it had long been felt in the trade that the wages
paid were not adequate to the requirements of the
men, looking at the laborious nature of their
occupation and the increased and increasing cost of
all the common necessaries of life. Feeling this,
an amalgamated committee, consisting of delegates
from each of the four societies of farriers in
London, had been formed to procure an advance
on the present rate of wages, and a memorial to
that effect had been sent in to the employers. The
result of the conference which had taken place
between the committee and the employers upon
that memorial would be laid before the meeting,
and its opinion taken upon the course it might be
necessary for the committee to pursue. He might
state, however, that if a strike was forced upon
them, no such step would be taken until the co-
operation of the Merlin's Cave Society had been
obtained, and he believed that society would be
represented upon the committee in the course of a
few days.
The Secretary then road the report of the com-
mittee, which stated that a few days after the
memorial had been sent to the employers the
committee received an invitation from Mr.
Stanley, the secretary of the employets, to meet
them at the Grosvenor Hotel. The committee
duly attended, but only six of its members were
admitted to the room, where they found 30
employers were assembled. Upon being asked
what advance of wages they required, the deputa-
tion stated they were there to request that in
future the wages of the firemen should be £2 per
week, and those of the doormen .£1 16s. per
week. This the employers at once refused, at the
same time treating the deputation in the most un-
courteous and disrespectful manner. The deputa-
tion then suggested as a compromise an advance
of 6d. per day all round, but this the employers
declined to grant, alleging that they had no power
to do so without consulting a general meeting,
which would be held in a fortnight from that
time. The deputation then loft, justly dissatisfied
with the manner in which they had been treated
amounting to insult. Three weeks had now
elapsed since the conference had taken place, and,
no communication of any sort having been re-

calved from the employers, the committee had
convened this general meeting of the trade. They
recommended that the suggestion for a com-
promise of an advance of ad. per day be now
withdrawn, and that the original demand be
strictly adhered to.
Mr. Williams moved:—

That, in the opinion of this meeting, the terms
asked by the committee—viz., a per week for
firemen, and .£1 16s. per week for doormen—are
fair and reasonable, and pledges itself to support
the committee in all means they may adopt to
obtain the same."

He stated that the employers had mired the depu-
tation a ragged and disrespectful lot of fellows
(shame). Ile, in reply, would say that the con-
duct of the employers towards the deputation was
simply disgraceful and unbecoming any body of
men laying claim to the title.of gentlemen (cheers).
They threatened a lock-out. In reply he would
say, let them beware that their conduct did not
provoke a strike (cheers.)
Mr. Wilson seconded the resolution, which was
carried.

articles.title: WHEELWRIGHTS, SMITHS, AND
articles.text:
WHEELWRIGHTS, SMITHS, AND

PAINTERS.

On Saturday evening a representative delegate
meeting of the above trades was held at the New
Inn, Old Bailey. Mr. Preston occupied the dila..
It was resolved that the Secretary should be
empowered to purchase the books required for
carrying out the movement of 10 per cent. advance
on piece work,:and the reduction of a week's work
to 54 hours.

Mr. Rider said as they were to memorialise
their employers, the question was to get things
prepared, and to appoint a time. He thought
they should form a sub-committee, and that a
meeting should be called about the month of
December, to which the masters should be
invited, so that the men should commence the nine
hours movement about the Ist of next March. He
thought that all resolutions passed by the sub-
committee should be presented before this com-
mittee, and afterwards considered by a general
meeting. He thought that the rules and dates of
the meetings should be printed on the back of the
contribution card.

It was proposed and carried to elect a sub-com-
mittee of twelve members, exclusive of the
chairman, and that eight should form a quorum.
By a majority, the following gentlemen were
elected :—Messrs. Rider, Bartlett, Howell, Thorn-
ley, Harvey, Sims, Bristo, Smallbone, Dwight,
Tompkins, Green, and Bridgett.
Mr. Bristo was elected assistant secretary.

It was stated that a member who had been
discharged for appearing on the platform in sup-
port of the movement had been reinstated—(cheers)
—and that the foreman who discharged him had
been discharged himself.

It was also stated that influence hai been used
against a member for alleged pieketting, and if
this should prove correct, it would be much to be
regretted.
The Secretary stated that 400 members had now
joined the movement.
After a vote of thanks to the chairman, the
proceedings closed.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

STAFFORDSHIRE.

of forming a jgdgment, a good deal remained to be
clone to raise the labouring classes of this country;
but ho did not think that either quarrying or the
coal pits were the most favourable kind of labour
with a view to mental elevation.

articles.title: THREATENED LOCK-OITT IN
articles.text:
THE THREATENED LOCK-OITT IN

SOUTH WALES.

On Saturday, at a meeting of ironworkers in
the neighbourhood of Wigan, addresses were deltw
vered by Mr. Kane, the general secretary to the ,
National Amalgamated Association of Ironworkers ;
and Mr. William Pickard, one of the English rO.
presentatives appointed by the Amalgamated Asso-
ciation of Miners to meet the South Wales masters.
The speakers made special reference to the
impending lock-out in the South Wales district,
and both suggested that in the struggle the iron-
workers and colliers should make common cause
against the employers.
Mr. Pickard said that the action of the masters
threatened the very existence of unionism in South
Wales. lie had been told that the ironworkers
there worked at a serious percentage below their
English and Scotch brethren, and the Wigan iron'
workeis, as well as the colliers, must be prepared
to deal with the matter and to support to the
utmost the men the masters were trying to crush.
The miners were ready to do this; 70,000 of them
were now banded together, and if ever they were
in a position to deal with a matter of this kind
they were now. They would use every effort to
come to an amicable arrangement, but the course
the masters had taken showed that the men must
be prepared for the worst.

Mr. Kane, replying to an assertion that the
unionists had been arbitrary in Wales, said that, if
anything, they had been too conciliatory. He held
it to be a pernicious thing that Welsh masters, who
were getting the same price for their work as those
in the North of England, should pay wages beloW
the English rate. If it was the intention of the
masters to persist in the lock-out unless the mee
withdrew from the union and forfeited their per-
sonal freedom, then, if it cost the union £lO,OOO '
it must withdraw the men from the district, and
send some of them, if necessary, to the United
States or Canada until the masters said they bad
had :enough. lie strongly advocated combined
action on the part of the ironworkers etta
colliers.

Resolutions were passed in favour of establish'
ing an arbitration board for a district to include
Manchester, Liverpool, Bolton, Preston, Warring'
ton, Garston, and Wigan; and deprecating Sunda/
labour.

articles.title: SOUTH YORKSHIRE NINERS' Atil*
articles.text:
SOUTH YORKSHIRE NINERS' Atil*

SOCIATION.

IMPORTANT ADDRESS TO THE MEMBERS'
The following address has been just issued to the

members :

FELLOWMEN,—When the rules and regulation%
of the association are being continually broken
and set at defiance with impunity, when
officers of the association are publicly insulted Itt
the presence of the employers, and when the care'
ful steady members of the association are prevent
from following their employment byed
the actions
of unthinking and unreasonable men, the meraberi
of your committee and council are bound to 151
the question before every member, in order that
the unanimous voice of the district may be raised
against sash unjust and illegal actions, and the
association may be saved from the ignominy which
would certainly be attached to it if the pooceeu,
lags of the Monk Bretton men were not denounced
in every part of the district.
The majority of our members will be aware
that this colliery is owned by Messrs. Embletoo,
Carter, Pepper, and Day. It was sunk by 3fr.
James Beaumont, of Oughtibridge, and the wee
joined our association as a lodge, in July, 1971'
immediately after having a dispute over the price
of straight work, which Mr. Normansell had bset!
the means of assisting them to settle. Forts time 51,1
went on very comfortably, but in the month 01
March last, a proper list of prices was requestou
by the workmen. Several meetings took Plec!t
but nothing satisfactory was agreed to, dad
was mutually arranged that such list ehould be leiD

to the arbitration of four practical working
colliers, who should try the work for a few
days, or a week, or so long as they required
to get a thorough knowledge of it, and
whatever prices they fixed should be paid
to the workmen. Accordingly, William Dearnley,
of East Gawber Colliery, and Amos Wood, of
Derby Main, were appointed on behalf of the
workmen, the owners appointing two men from the
Warren Vale Colliery,lone of the oldest union
collieries in the district. The four men worked in
the different places in the pit, and at the end of
14 days mutually agreed upon a list of prices
which they believed to be just between both par-
ties, and although the question had been decided
by four members of the Miners' Association, the
Monk Bretton men refused to accept the decision,
and struck against it, and when one of the district
secretaries went to a meeting of the men in com-
pany with the two arbitrators, to explain their
reasons for giving the award, they were accused
of selling the workmen, and insulted in every
possible manner although the arbitrators declare
that they can make very good wages at the prices
fixed. _ _

This strike lasted three days, at the end of
which time the men resumed work at the prices
fixed, and ever since a bad feeling has existed
among the men against the association and its
officers, and against the employers, and even
against themselves. Thore has scarcely been a
month but there has been one or two strikes over
little petty matters that are not worth five
minutes' consideration, and which has entailed a
serious loss to the owners, and is driving every
steady sensible man away from the colliery to seek
work somewhere else. Now, be it observed, that
not one single complaint has over been laid before
the council of the association from those men, of
anyidescription whatever, and, as the rules dis-
tinctly state that no colliery shall take any action
of this nature without the knowledge and consent
of every lodge in the district, after which it must
be sanctioned by the council, your committee feel
bound in justice to the owners of the colliery, in
justice to the association, and for the sake of the
steady workers, who are suffering from the tyranny
of unreasonable men, to enter their solemn protest
against such proceedings.
During the last three weeks there has been
three strikes at the colliery, and when one of the
officers of the association heard of the second
strike by common report, he went to the house
where the lodge is held for the purpose of ascer-
taining what was the matter in dispute. Upon
enquiring for the cheek-weighman, in the hope of
getting the information he required from him, he
was told that he (the check-weightnan) had gone
up to the colliery office in order to hear what was
the matter in dispute; the first person he saw
was a man as usual at the head of the deputation,
and who had only worked at the place three weeks.
Another person of the same deputation was on
notice to leave, and had only a week to stay at the
colliery, and in the interview he told the employers
that the district officers did not do their duty, that
the men would not work any more until the things
they complained of were rectified, and conducted
himself in such an insolent, overbearing manner as
to insult every one of the employers, and bring
discredit upon the whole association. During the
afternoon of the same day it was arranged that the
men should commence and continuo at work, and
a deputation, along with Mr. Normansell, would
meet the owners on the following Thursday, but
on the very day the interview was to be hold,
another strike took place, and the whole matter
was again upset. Under these circumstances
your committee and council have passed the follow-
ing resolution, which they recommend to the
attention of the members of the association, and
cannot too strongly urge upon them the necessity
of using very strong measures to put a atop to their
actions :

Resolved, that this committee having heard the
statement of the district secretaries in reference to
the illegal proceedings of the Monk Bretton men,
is of opinion that their past and present conduct
is most reprehensible, so much so that the associa-
tion is bound to take some immediate action to
put a stop to the proceedings which are now prac-
tised by them, and with a view of giving a true
and proper exposition of the whole affair, this
committee instructs the district secretaries to issue
circulars explaining the whole of the ease to every
lodge in the district, with power to use their own
discretion to publish the same in any public news-
paper they may consider advisable, in order- to
clear the association from being accused of parti-
cipating in such conduct, and with a view of
putting a stop to such proceedings in the future.
This resolution has received the unanimous
sanction of the council since passed by the com-
mittee.

The raembers of the committee and co-incil ars
perfectly aware that upon every occasion the em-
ployers and manager of the Monk. Bretton Colliery
have shown every disposition to deal openly, can-
didly, and fuirly with the workmen, and when the

men and their association have such an opportu-
nity of settling any real complaint that may arise
at the colliery, we feel confident that there is not
the slightest cause for the men to conduct them-
selves in the disgraceful manner they are doing,
and should such conduct be persisted in, the asso-
ciation will most assuredly assist the employers in
bringing them before the magistrates for compen-
sation, and as an example to others, for breach of
contract of service between them and their em-
ployers, as the members of the committee and
council are determined to put an end to all such
illegal proceedings, for it is plain that when men
abuse the power which organization gives them,
they furnish one of the strongest arguments that
the opponents of trades unions can require, and
they become the greatest tyrants it is possible to
conceive. The members of the committee and
council of the association, believing that it was
established to protect its members from injustice,
cannot allow any section of those members to per-
petrate injustice upon others. They are desirous
of speaking with no uncertain sound in this case,
and they sincerely hope it will be the means of
restoring that peace and discipline at the colliery
which is so essentially necessary for the comfort
and welfare of employers and workmen; and it is
with a deep sense of the responsibility attaching
to the subject that it has been brought before the
notice of the members; but as every sensible man
knows that this state of things cannot possibly
exist without bringing disgrace upon the associa-
tion, it is requested that every member will exert
his influence to alter it; and while we are on a
subject we have always sot our faces against, we
take the opportunity of saying to every member
of the association that the tide of prosperity in our
coal trade is turning, and unless men will be more
guided by sound wisdom and counsel, the good
and true men of the association will have to suffer
with the bad. Hence the necessity of every sen-
sible man protesting against the illegal and reck-
less proceedings at Monk Bretton, and wherever
wrong may be done to the men by:eithor employer
or manager, the associatiOn is in such a position
now as will put any real complaint right without
the colliery being idle a single day.
By order of the committee and council, we are,
yours obediently,
J. NORMA/MEM., I Secretaries.
P. CASEY,
Nelson-street, Barnsley, Oct. 7th, 1872.

articles.title: SOCIAL SCIENCE IN GERMANY,
articles.text:
SOCIAL SCIENCE IN GERMANY,

IMPORTANT DISCUSSION ON TRADRS UNIONS.

The subject of Strikes has occupied the Congress
just held at Eisenach. On Tuesday Professor
Scbmollor, of Halle, the same who had delivered
the inaugural speech, came forward to com-
municate his views on the important topic of the
day. Ho said :
The strikes were a necessary consequence of the
laws abolishing guilds. Masters being no longer
connected with the men by ties of common interest,
honour, and camaraderie, naturally regarded their
assistants as strangers, and were intent upon
making as much money as possible out of them.
The working classes would be utterly impotent to
resist the exactions to which they wet() subjected
had they not acquired the right of combining
against their employers. The Trade Unions were
the best form which these combinations could
assume. Being permanent societies, and having'
for their object not only the organization of strikes,
but also the education of the working man and the
dispensing of relief in sickness and need, these
Unions were mostly directed by respectable men,
and did as much to prevent uncalled-for strikes as
they did to organize legitimate ones. The longest
and most disorderly strikes that had occurred in
Germany had broken out in localities were Trade
Unions were unknown and Socialism was in the
ascendant. This moderating influence exercised
by the Trade Unions, as well as the many other
commendable objects pursued by them, ought to
induce Government to accord them corporate
rights, lie could not, however, deny that strikes,
though unavoidable, were an evil, and that means
should be taken to render them as rare as possible.
He therefore advocated the institution of Boards
of Arbitration and Conciliation. The members of
those Boards might be elected by masters and men
alike, but once duly installed, they ought to possess
the power assigned to the other and more learned
courts of justice officiating in this country. He
likewise thought it desirable to appoint separate
courts, also of an elective character, to decide all
disputes between masters and men, excepting such
as referred to wages. He did not conceal from
himself that it would take some time to impress
the public with the necessity of these changes, and
he would, therefore, specially advocate some altera-
tions in the existing laws, which he had much at
heart. The labouring man being so much more
disadvantageously situated than the capitalist,
wanted certain concessions to enable him to sustain
the struggle for existence with any chance of
success. lie therefore proposed that the law
holding the labouring matt responsible for breach
of contract with his employer should be abolished.
He also suggested the propriety of permitting
Trade Unions to spend their funds in strikes, not
even excepting that portion contributed for purposes
of relief. lie, furthermore, would liberate all
working men belonging to Trade Unions, and con-
tributing to the relief funds of these societies, from
the duty now legally imposed upon them of paying
in to Own° publio relief fund,

This speech, delivered in the most impressiv e
style, and with a rare command of choice and ele
gant phraseology, was not thrown away upon the
audience. Seldom, indeed, has so dry and grave a
theme been treated in a more attractive form.
Still, though the Professor's auguments were less
methodically grouped than the abstract above
given, it did not escape the hearers that there was
many an ugly snake concealed beneath the rank
verbiage of the flowery orator. The audience,
indeed, regarded it as only fair that the working
classes should remain possessed of the right to
strike, seeing that capitalists likewise enjoyed the
privilege of combining for their own advantage.
Most of those present were moreover convinced
that it would be equally venturesome to withdraw
the right to strike from the German workman as
to snatch food out of the lion's mouth. The Pro-
fessor's wish, too, that Trade Unions should be
conceded the rights of corporate bodies was pretty
unanimously applauded; and, indeed, if strikes
are really inevitable, it is better that they should
be directed by organized societies 'conscious of
their responsibility to the public and themselves,
than by agitators pursuing extravagant or egotistic
ends. But when the Professor coolly intimated
that the working classes should be permitted to
break contracts with impunity, if they thought
thereby to get the better of their employers, the
meeting, so long amenable to his persuasive
representations, began to manifest a different tone.
When he went the length of asserting that the
same classes should be first freed from the duty of
contributing towards public relief funds, and then
expressly permitted to consume their own private
relief funds in fighting their employers, the irrita-
tion of his hearers reached a height which vented
itself in frequent cries and groans. People now
perceived that, though the Professor repudiated
Socialism, he went very near the dangerous abyss;
indeed, they were dismayed to see that, not content
with equalizing the laws for all classes alike, he
thought it compatible with justice to accord to one
section of society impunity for a peculiarly sordid
kind of offence, actionable in the case of all others.
Some persons could not trust their ears when they
heard the labouring man positively encouraged to
regard his employer as a sort of outlaw, and to
squander his savings in the social struggle, relying
upon society to set him on his legs again through
the public relief officer, if the worst came to the
worst. Sentiments like these could not be forced
upon such a meeting, albeit clothed in the most
refined of diction.
A landed proprietor, Herr Kauer, rose to tell the
speaker that if his propositions should ever become
law, order would soon after have to be restored by
grapeshot and the running fire of needle-guns.
A professor of law, Herr von Holtzendorff,
protested against the ideas of his indiscreet
colleague, reminding the assembly that if the field
hands were to be exempt from keeping their word
immense loss was likely to arise in harvest time.
Dr. Engel, the chief of the Prussian Statistical
Department, maintained that workmen breaking
their contracts should not alone be held responsible
for damages as was now the case, but in the event
of their inability to pay, imprisoned. The worst
excrescences of the professorial wisdom having
thus been pruned off, the opportunity was seized
for inquiring into the nature of the recent strikes.
Dr. Hirsch and Herr Duneker, the representa-
tives of the German Trade Unions, declared that
their societies numbered already 1,200,000
members, and that far from regarding the
organization of strikes as their exclusive object,
they eudeavoured to educate and relieve the work-
men as well. The Trade Unions, moreover, wore
opposed to Socialism, and would be delighted to hear
that the present meeting had resisted the tempta-
tion of entertaining any schemes at variance with
the sacred and manly principle of self .help. These
gentlemen also regretted the notion advanced by
a Prussian ultra-Conservative that the labour
system ought to be remodelled in a semi-Com-
munistic, semi-Absolutist way by the Royal
dynasties of the country.
Herr Kauer, the landed proprietor who had so
bluntly spoken his mind before, observed that the
Trade Unions might be all very well in their way,
but that it would be much better if employers and
employed could be induced to love and respect
each other as Christians, than to continue the
strife.

Dr. lilac, permanent counsel for the Berlin
Building Masters' Society, supported by one of
his colleagues, complained that their men were
daily becoming more lazy and more restive. A
journeyman bricklayer, for instance, who a few
years ago, when receiving half his present wages,
had set up 800 bricks a day, now with a double
rate of pay set up only 200. Still worse, the men
were constantly breaking agreements, running
away from the work, and getting up partial and
general strikes, regardless of contracts. TheY

5

well knew that they were too poor to be held
responsible for damages. Neither the professor
who had addressed the assembly in the interests
of philanthropical improvement, nor the distin-
guished men who endeavoured to direct and
moderate the Trade Unions, knew what a strike
really meant. No doubt it was sometimes set on
foot with a view to satisfy the pressing needs of
the workmen, and in such a case was legitimate.
But much more frequently strikes were indulged
in from a wish to embarrass masters, and to
manifest the hatred against the well-to-do classes
rife in the working population. Many of the
men were very well aware that the strike of one
trade must call forth the strike of another, and

that, in consequence, though wages were raised,
they did not go much further than formerly.
_ _

These assertions were all but directly confirmed
by Herr Ranisch, a journeyman engineer, and the
chairman of a large Trade Union in Berlin. The
labourers, he said, were tired of working without
a prospect of rising. They daily saw capitalists
getting on in the world, however small the sum
originally at their disposal, and they did not know
why they alone should be excluded from the
chance of attaining independence. That the
strikes would very much advance their views was
of course improbable. But the Trade Unions had
a much more comprehensive object than to raise
wages, and therefore deserved the support of all
who wished to further the intelligence, culture,
and self-reliance of the workmen.

The debate having thus swayed to and fro for
some time, Professor Gneist, the famous jurist, who
had been elected president, vacated the chair, pre-
paratory to taking part in the discussion. In a
masterly speech he gave a succinct digest of the
various opinions expressed, and declared in favour
of free trade, free coalition, and a somewhat com-
plicated system of institutions intended to mediate
between masters and men. He preferred an orga-
nized war between capitalists and Trade Unions
to the Montenegrin razzias undertaken by Social-
ists. Ile would therefore recommend the introduc-
tion of a Trade Union law wherever the local
authorities thought it advisable. In conclusion, he
gave it as his deliberate conviction that, though no
pains should be spared to reconcile conflicting in-
terests in a friendly way, it would be altogether
impracticable to attempt to change the working of
the laws of property "as disoovered and laid down
by the immortal Adam Smith." This was too much
for the professors of nee-political economy who
had originated the Congress. Had they obtaimd
Professor Gnoist's signature to tbeir letters of 'in-
vitation only to be bearded by him in their own
haunt? Had they secured the support of so many
other unsuspecting men merely to hear them ap-
plaud the eulogium bestowed upon the odious
originator of a school so vehemently combatect
by thorn? "Very false" cried one, the moment
the heterodox words escaped the lips of Professor
Gueist. " Very untrue " ejaculated another.
" What next ? " sarcastically added a third. But
they saw which way the wind blew; having, no
doubt, ere this, realised that Professor Gneist had
the vast majority of the meeting on his side, they
did not try to vindicate their partioulas doctrines
again.

Accordingly Professor Schmoller in his reply
confined himself to asserting that the prceeding
speaker was virtually at one with him, though ho
had seemingly expressed himself in such a different
way. He added that he and his friends were
actuated by a wish to mediate and conciliate hi
all they did, whereas the language held by some
manufacturers tended to foment rebellion.
His words had no power to change the conclu-
sions the meeting had already formed rcspeetinz
the soundness of the teachings of himself and
friends. Instead of the very specific and ex-
travagant propositions recommended by Professors
Schmoller and Brentano, the meeting adopted
the following general and temperate resolutions
I. FACTORY LAWS.

_
1. The German Factory Laws are framed in
accordance with the requirements of the Case, but
should be more effectually tarried out by (Acura
appointed by the State.
2. The German Factory Laws require to be
supplemented by other statutes still further
reducing the hours of work for young persons
and enforcing attendance. at school. Whenever
the evils these laws are intended to remedy show
themselves, regulations adapted to the special re-
gulations adapted to the ibpwial requirements of
the various trades should be passed.
3. It is necessary to enact similar special laws
for married women.
IL COALITION LAWS.

1. The right to combine for the attainment of 0,
common purpose is to be unconditionally re-
cognised and maintained.
2. The majority of the meeting are of opinion
that the Trade Umons and the relief fonds they
collect should be recognised by the law, provided
certain conditions and obligations are complied •
with.

3. The institution of Boards of Arbitrat4ort
and Conciliation is dsclared to bo useful.

Assembly, will, it is said, be followed up by
M. Ilonher by an appeal to the Council of
State.

Marshal Bazaine's inBtructum, preparatory
to the trial, proceeds somewhat cumbrously.
Several new incidents in it are reported by a
correspondent at Versailles. Among the
general opinions and speculations to which the
trial gives rise, what is most striking is the
unusual distaste of the Army for having the
odious history of Metz raked up again.

Prince Bismarck's furlough has been the sub-
ject of discussion among German journalists,
some of whom affirmed that it had. been pro-
longed an special application for three months.
The semi-official organ, which enunciates what
the Prince wishes to be believed, set them
right with the explanation that the furlough
was indefinite, but that it is not likely to last
another three months.

An emphatically Imperialist platform has
been laid down by the new Minister President
of Hesse Darmstadt. He affirmed inter alia
that the interests of the Ducal house, as well
as those of the country, were to be best served
by fulfilling their duties toward the Empire.

Baron Beaulieu, who retires from the
Belgian Embassy in London, will be succeeded
by M. Henry Solvyers, now Minister Pleni,
potentiary of Belgium at the Court of Rome.

Lord Northbrook is performing his first
autumn tour with great suavity and accept-
ance Be started from Simla on the 11th,
and intended travelling by way of Umballa to
Bombay. In consequence of choleraic infec-
tion among the villages surounding Umballa
it was not thought expedient to hold a durbar
there. This change in the ordinary Viceregal
programme has thrown a tine opportunity, in
the way of Bombay, where the durbar will be
held instead of at Umballa,

An interesting trait of modern Japan figures
in the last mail news. During his visit to
Nagaski, the Mikado waited upon the telegraph
operators, with the intention of exchanging
civilities with the crowned heads of Europe.
On discovering that even electricity may keep
a man waiting longer than he has time to
spare, he relinquished the project.

In congratulating Sir noun(lell Palmer on
Ins accession to the Lord Chancellorship, the
County justices of Oxford observe 'that he is the
Only Oxfordshire man, with the exception of
Simon Lord Harcourt, who has attained that
legal eminence.

• Sir David Baxter, of Hiimam, who has for
several months been in feeble health, died the
other day on his estate near Cupar. His
memory as a philanthropist will live in the
public park at Dundee, and in the Science
Scholarships at Edinburgh University, both of
which are identified with his name. His cont.
meroial reputation lived. untarnished through
all the fluctuations and vicissitudes of more
than half a century. His nephew, the Secre-
tary to the Treasury, will succeed him in the
baronetcy.

At the Oxfordshire Quarter Sessions on
Ifond.ay the magistrates resolved to increase
the pay of the constabulary, from the deputy
chief constable downwards, ten per cent., in
consequence of the increased price of provi-
sions.

John Dorrington, MA., M.D., &0,, master
of-a college in Derbyshire, has been summoned
by the Charity- Organization Sooiety for an
"urgent appeal to the benevolent" on behalf
of a lady whose self-sacrificing devotion to her
parents had rendered her unable to support
herself in her old age. It is estimated that
Mr. Dorrington has, during several years,
realised £6,000 out of this very touching case,
all the more creditable to him as the self-
sacrificing lady was his own sister. But, in
one particular, his ciroular was inexact, as
the lady was keeping house for a gentleman
and earning good wages. He was committed
for trial without bail.

A Tiampstead tutor who struck a constable
over the head with his stick for declining to
cross the street and show him which was" go.
8," has been fined 485., with the alternative
Of a month's imprisonment.

M. Emile 011ivier, who has been so long
withdrawn from public attention has just
published a work entitled "A. Visit to the
msdiei Chapel, and a Dialogue betiveen
Michael Angelo and Raphael."

'Monday's Journal °field mentions the re-
port which had recently been circulated in the
French press, that 31. Picard, the representa-
the of France in Belginm, had resigned his
post. "This news,'' adds the official organ,
"is not correct, and never has been" It
appears that M. Thiers really received a letter
purporting to come from Id. Picard, an-
nouncing his resignation; but the letter
proved to be a forgery.

Dr. Manning will, it is believed.; have a.
coadjutor assigned to him. This honour is
destined for the Right Rev. : Monsignor
Weathers, Rector of St. Thomas Seminary,
Hammersmith, and one of the oanonists who
framed the, definition of Papal. Infallibility
submitted to the Einimenical

Prince Albrecht of Prussia died on Monday
evening.

All the persons charged at St. Etienne, with
being members of the " Alliance Itepabli-
caine," supposed to be a secret society, have
been acquitted.

The funeral of Mr. Seward took place on
Monday at Auburn. Several thousand visitors
wore present. President Grant has addressed
a telegram to General Seward condoling with
him, and speaking of the death of Mr. Seward
as a loss to; the nation. He says the late
lamented statesman's services to the country
have becotne a part of its history.

An improvement is about to be made in the
western portion of St, Paul's-churchyard. The
dwarf wall of stone which now surrounds the
cathedral facing Ludgate-hill, with the solid
iron railings with which it is crowned, will be
removed as far as the north-west and south-
east corners of the fabric itself, and the entire
area or court-yard, in the centre of which
stands the statue of Queen Anne, will be thrown
open to the bottom of the steps which lead, up
to the great western door.

While a sale was being carried on at Mr.
Curtis's, of Silver-street, Lincoln, on Tuesday,
the floor gave way, and several persons were
preeipitated into a cellar below. Some of them
were seriously injured, and the auctioneer,
Mr. Shepperd, received a severe fracture of the

The brokerage on purchase and sale of in-
vestments under the Court of Chancery in the
year ended the 31st of March last was £10,873
is. 7d.

Another Cabinet Council was held on Monday
afternoon, and was attended by all the
Ministers in town, except Mr. Forster, who
was prevented attending by indisposition.

The Secretary of State for War has directed
that in the present and future years the
Volunteer year shall terminate on the 31st of
Ootober instead of the 20th November.

Mr. Massey, the Liberal candidate for
Tiverton, addressing a meeting of the electors
on Monday!, said ft Conservative working man
was "either an embodiment of most exalted
Christian charity, or else the meanest sneak
that could disgrace the class to which he be-
longed,"

A n old lady named Mrs. Heaton was
burned to death in her own house, at Raven.
hurst- street, Birmingham, on Tuesday
last. She and her husband lived together,
the old lady being 72, and Mr. Heaton 80
years of age. It ursupposed that her dress
caught fire when she was boiling some water.
Her dress and underclothing were almost
burnt a way, and on one side of her body from
the head to the foot,' the flesh was literally
charred to the bone.

At a meeting of the Norwich Town Council
on Tuesday, the Mayor read a letter from the
Lord Chancellor, intimating his intention to
remove Mr. Blake and Major Bignold from the
Commission •of the Peace for Norwich, in
consequence of the late fracas on the Norwich
Bench.

A man named Thud,' Crowley, was oharged
at Dromod Petty Sessions on Tuesday with
entering: into a conspiracy to shoot Major
Gore, M.P. in the year 1863. One of the con-
spirators and others gave evidence. The
prisoner was committed for trial at the next
Leitrim Assizes.

On Tuesday morning Sarah Beal, an elderly
woman, living a lonely life ot Nither-green,
near Sheffield, was found by a policeman
burned to death by her own fireside, her
clothes being in ashes and her body
horribly charred.

The Quarter Sessions for the borough of
Rochester held on ruesclay, was a maiden
session, an event which has not occurred for
some years. The Mayor, Mr. Woodhams,
presented the Recorder, Mr. Barrow, with a
pair of white gloves, and made some remarks
as to the satistectoig working of the Licensing
Act, in which the Recorder conourred.

Penny school -fees have engaged. the atten-
tion of the Liverpool School Board, and it is
proposed to erect a temporary school for the
purpose of an experiment.

At the Westminster Police-court, on Mon-
day, John Leary, a lad of eighteen, and John
M'Grale' charged with being drunk and re-
fusing to quit the Nell Gwynne Tavern, in
Grosvenor-row, and with assaulting a police-
man who was called in to eject them, were
sentenced, the former to four months, and the
latter to one mouth's imprisonment and hard
labour.

The death is announced of Sir David Baxter,
the eminent Dundee merchant. He was uno!e
to Mr. W. E. Baxter, ALP., one of the Secretaries
to the Treasury.

The Morley Main Colliery was re-opened on
Monday, having been reported to be in a safe
condition.

A destructive fire broke out at Darfield Main
Colliery, near Barnsley, on Monday, necessi-
tating the closing of the pit.

The first rail of the East Suffolk tramway
was laid on Monday, at Great Yarmouth, by
Sir E. H. K. Lawn, M.P.

A correspomjent in Madrid says that very
little importance is attached there to the rising
which has taken place at Ferrol. The move-
ment appears to be purely local, and the
Government announces that it will be soon
put down. Telegrams from Madrid meanwhile
state that the insurgents are in a state of
anarchy, that they, have pillaged the provision
cellars at the Arsenal, are much discouraged,
and not likely to hold out if attacked.

Mr. Webb, the American Consul at Zanzi-
bar, has received a letter from Dr. Living-
stone, dated Unyamyembe, July 2. Mr.
Webb says that Dr. Livingstone appears to
have learnt that Mr. Stanley had sent a party
to assist him in his nudei taking, and was loud
in his praise of this energy and. kindness.
Nothing had been heard of Mr. Stanley's exi
pedition since t left Zanzibar.

A young Englishman has just died in Chur
from the effects of drinking of the water of
the Roseg glacier. He was advised by his
tutor not to partake of it, but did so, and
dig after four days' illness.

• The Iron WorkeT of Messrs. Johnstone, in
Pennsylvania, the largest in America, have
been burned. The loss is estimated at
500,000 dols.

The Bishop of Lincoln has issued a form of
prayer for use in his diocese, supplicating the
Divine aid for the removal of the cattle disease
now so prevalent.

Prince Hassan, the eldest son of the
Khedive of Egypt, has finished his Oxford
career, and he will, it is said, make a three
years' tour round the world.

Messrs. Macmillan and Co. announce an
Ilustrated Mistory of Holland House, by the
Princess Marie von Lichtenstein, nee Fox, the
adopted and recently married daughter of Lady
Holland.

The gross receipts of the Woods, Forests,
and Land Revenues. of the Crown were, in the
last year, £482,596 Bs. 7d., and after the ex-
penditure of 375,000 was paid into the Ex-
chequer.

At the close of the French and German war,
quantities of seed potatoes were sent from
Great Britain to enable the half-ruined French
farmers, whose lands had been oyerrun by the
contending armies, to produce a crop for the
ensuing year. Part of the second year's pro-
duce of those seed potatoes is now being
shipped for the English market.

From a financial statement presented by the
clerk to the Leeds School Board it appears
that the current expenditure of the Board, in-
cluding office expenses, amounts to about
44,000 per annum. This is an addition to the
fees paid by children and the Government
grant. A rate at three-halfpence in the pound
covered the cost.

In London
.2,135 births and 1,218 deaths
were registered last week. Alter making
allowance for increase of population, the births
were 124 and the deaths 214 below the average
numbers in the corresponding period of the
last ten years. The annual rate of mortality
was 19 per 1,000 in London, 24 in Portsmouth,
27 in Birmingham, 28 in Manchester, and 20
in Newcastle-on-Tyne. The 1,218 deaths in
London included 7 from small-pox, 7 from
measles) 21 from scarlet fever, 31 from (litre-
rent forms of fever, and 45 from diarrhces.

Sir Robert Canhire was sleeted for the Flint
Boroughs on Tuesday without opposition.

The fey. John Parches, of St. James's,
Brighton, is reported. to be in a critical state.

Oct 19,1 1872.

Their Royal Highnesses the Prince and
Princess of Wales have been met with the
heartiest expressions of loyalty in Northum-
berland. At a shooting party held on Wednes-
day, the Prince and those who accompanied
him were successful in obtaining good bags of
game.

A sharp rejoinder has been given to the
Roman Catholic bishops' manifesto at tbo
Fulda Congress. The Provincial Correspond-
ence intimates that it is high time to draw a
has between Chit and ecclesiastical affairs,
from the civil side.

Friendly intervention has brought the
Laurium mines dispute to the verge of settle-
ment. The negotiations which have been ill
progress with this view will, it is hoped, be
speedily completed at Rome.

Mr. Secretary Fish has exacted a veryftUt
promise of satisfaction from the Mexican .
authorities in respect of the recent
raids. All the property stolen is to be restored
forthwith, and the rivers are to be surrendered
as early as may be. frontier

A curate in the Diocese of Peterborough-- ;
the Rev. Peter Robson—varied the service a
few Sundays ago by challenging an agrji"
cultural labourer to tight. After a good de'
of provocation, the latter accepted, and severel
rounds were executed in presence of the
congregation, who could not get into church.
The curate has been reported by the Bench to'
his Bishop.

Mrs. James Austin whose husband Ina
something to do with the advertising depart-
ment of the Gallery of Illustration, having been
deprived of his society for several days, went
to his place of business to look after him. 11°
received her with a brutal blow on the ePP
which knocked her down insensible. At Marl-
borough-street Police Court he was thought •
worthy of four months' imprisonment, with
hard labour.

We regret to announce that Emily, Coulteso
of Shaftesbury, wife of Anthony Ashlef
Cowper, seventh Earl of Shaftesbury) died'
somewhat unexpectedly on Tuesday forenoon
at the family residence in Grosvenor-squaro.
The much-lamented lady, who leaves a large
family, was the eldest daughter of the lato
Viscountess Palmerston, by her first husband,
the Earl Cowper, and sister of the-Right Hon.
W. P. Cowper-Temple, M.P., and uf the Hon.
Spencer Cowper.

There has been a general breakdown in 00
prosecution of the Alliance Republicaine in St.
Etienne, the police not having obtained a single
conviction.

Papal addresses to deputations have of late
assumed an interesting historical tinge.
The other day in a homily which the Pope do
livered to certain Transteverian pilgrims, Nvii°
washed their hands before him of all the sacri-
lege of the 20th September and the 2ua
October, he observed moarnfully that even the
House of Savoy had produced saints in its
time, and that England had once enjoyed the
rule of a devout Prince like Edward the
Sixth.

At the annual conference in the Manchester
Free Trade Hall, on Tuesday, the United
Kingdom Alliance passed a resolution hailiff;
the new Licensing Act" as a sign of progress
but some of the speakers qualified the coin-
mendation by alluding to it as a pieee of patoh-
work business. Sir Wilfrid Lawson alarmed
that the Permissive Bill wai the very least
which would ever be accepted. He propoPed
starting Permissive Bill candidates for ever/
vacant seat in Parliament; but dissension
arose out of an apprehension entertained bY
sundry delegates that it was intended to divert
part of the £90,000 guarantee fund to ele°'
tioneering purposes.

After inspecting thirteen batteries of
artillery under a heavy fog on Woolwioh"
common, his Royal Highness the Corainandar-
in-ohief distributed the prizes to the cadets Ati
Woolwioh Academy on Tuesday. Gencrftr
Napier's report on the short-time system
education was exceedingly favourable.
