A grand public breakfast was giVen
A.berystwith on Tuesday, in celebration Oft
opening of the University College of Wfar
Colonel Pryse, the Lord-Lieutenant of 0°
county, presided, and offered his congratula-
tions on the opening of the college, which ll°
said, whould, provide a good education for the
people of Wales, and place the Welsh on All
equality with other nations. -

On Tuesday morning the new tuxret-slaP
Devastation steamed out of Portsmouth
harbour, for the contractor's trial of 11
engines. After having run for a couple 0
miles off Spithead at half-speed with great
ease, full speed was turned on, sad not Joni
afterwards a flaw appeared in the hot-well
each engine, which necessitated their bailiff
stopped. The damage is expected to be
repaired in three weeks.

Great alarm was experienced by the passen-
gers in the express train travelling through
the Dawlish Tunnel on Monday night, caused
by heavy bumpings on the top of the carriages,
and the smashing in of one side of a second-
class carriage. The train was stopped, and it
was found that both connecting rods of the
engine had broken. Another engine arriving,
the train was taken off safely.

A special Midland train ran into a Great
Western passenger train on Tuesday at Barn.
wood Junction, about nine miles from
Gloucester, by which nine persons were
injured.

The ease of' the Tiohborne Claimant came
before Mr. Justice Quoin, in chambers on
Tuesday, on a summons calling on Messrs.
Gorton and De Fiva, who have been his
attorneys, to deliver to the Claimant all docu-
ments in their custody relating to his defence.
The application was resisted, on the ground
that the solicitors had a lien on the papers
until their bill of costs had been paid. The
trustees of the Defence Fund were ready to pay
the amount on taxation, but the bill could not
be taxed until after tho vacation. Ultimately,
it was arranged that the matter should be
referred to Master Pollock.

• A series of meetings on the high price of
food, for the purpose of pressing the subject
upon the attention of the Legislature, are
being arranged to be held in various parts of
the metropolis. Deputations from the Anti-
Game Law League will attend these meetings
to expose the influence of the Game Laws on
the production of food.

Some of the cab proprietors in Manchester
have raised their fares to is. per mile for any
number of passengers, the fares hitherto
charged having been 9d. per mile for one or
two passengers and is. for any number above.
The reason assigned for the advance is the in-
creased cost of wages and materials.

At a Court held on Tuesday at Balmoral,
Lord thitherley had audience of her Majesty,
and resigned the Great Seal, which was there-
upon consigned by her Majesty to the keeping
of Sir Roundell Palmer, who was sworn of the
Privy Council, and appointed Lord Chancellor.
At the Privy Council, held on the same day,
Parliament was further prorogued till the 19th
December.

The debate on the subject of gratuitous
education of the children of the poor was
resumed at the weekly meeting of the London
School Board on Wednesday, and was again
adjourned. The general tone of the debate
was adverse to the proposition.

On Wednesday afternoon the remains of
Sir George Pollook, Bart., G.C.8., G.C.5.1.,
the late Constable of the Tower, were deposited
in Westminster Abbey. The coffin was
brought from the deceased's residence,
Clapham-common, on a gun-carriage. A
large number of officers of all grades, including
his .Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge,
who had assembked at the Westminster Palace
Hotel, joined the cortege as it passed, and
formed part of the procession in the Abbey.
The religious ceremony was conducted by the
sub-Dean Rev. Lord john Thynne, the Von.
Arohdeacon Jennings, and the Rev. Canon
Conway.

The memorial stone of the North Cambridge-
shire Cottage Hospital at Wisboach was laid
on Wednesday by Miss E. Trafford Southwall,
who has given the land, and proposes to
endow the hospital with £3,000.

The district board of Greenwich having re-
fused to pay the London. School Board rate,
notice has been given that legal proceedings
will be taken to enforce the order. If the
amount due should not be paid in a short time
proceedings will be taken in the Court of
Queen's Bench.

Thomas Trice, cab-driver, was brought up
at the Mansion-house Police-court on Tuesday,
charged with causing the death of an elderly
woman named Mary Jones, by running over
her with his cab. He was committed for
trial, but admitted to bail.

It is stated that the movement in aid of the
Irish Church, initiated by
.the Archbishop of
Canterbury, has resulted m the collection of
£43,000, which will be partially applied to
the Episcopal Endowment Fund, and partly
to the fund for the assistance of poor parishes.

It is rumoured in Dublin thnt Cardinal
Cullen and the Roman Catholio Bishops will
theet on the return of his Eminence from
Rome, and that they will issue a manifesto as
to education and other public questions,

It would appear that the Spanish Govern-
ment is still unwilling to employ force against
the insurgents at Ferrol. The municipality
of the town has asked for a delay of a day,
pending negotiations ; and it is thought that
the men will lay down their arms, and blood-
shed be thus avoided,

THE WORKING MEN'S CO-OPERATIVE

COLONY.

The sixth half-yearly meeting of the Mutual
Land Emigration and Co-operative Coloniza-
tion Company (Limited), was hold at their
office, 18, Denmark-street, Soho, on Wednes-
day evening, October 9th, Mr. Charles
Murray, chairman, presidiitg.
The Chairman briefly, reviewed the progress
made by the company during the past twelve
months, and said that by persistency and
energy, the time would soon draw nigh, when
the position of the company would be such as
to redound to the credit of the shareholders,
and be an example it would be well for other
societies to follow.
The third annual balance sheet was then
submitted, showing an income of £327, and an
expenditure of £320. It was shown that the
working expenses of the company had been
carried on chiefly by voluntary contributions
by the members, thus leaving the greater
portion of the money subscribed for shares to
be invested in the land. The assets of the
company were also favourable.
The directors' and auditors' report, together
with the balance sheet, were unanimously
accepted.
The chairman and retiring directors were
re-elected, and auditors appointed for ensuing
half year. Mr. H. Cowing was appointed
financial secretary, and Mr. J. Rogers as cor-
responding secretary.
A vote of thanks to the officers for past
services was carried by acclamation.
The attention of all working men interested
in the political and social regeneration of man-
kind is called to the above undertaking,
which is founded for the purpose of
putting into operation just laws on land, credit,
currency, and. exchange, and have acquired a
tract of land (720 acres) in Kansas, U.S.A., to
be the scene of operations. Meetings are held
at the above place every Sunday evening, for the
purpose of explaining the objects and prin-
ciples of the company. Chair taken at quarter
to seven.

Through the foundering of a steamer in
Lake Michigan four persons have been drowned
and two boatloads of the survivors are still
missing.

Speaking at Langres in connection with the
inauguration of a monument to the fallen
Mobiles of that locality, the Prince de Joinville
has thrown out a happy suggestion for filling
the vacanay at the top of the proposed new
Vendome Colamn. He should like to see
there the simple statue of a French soldier.

The Prince of Wales, it is stated, is about
to pay a visit to Warwickshire and become
the gust of the Earl of Aylesford, at Packing-
ton Park.

The case of Michael Davitt, one of the
Fenian prisoners, who is alleged to have been
treated with undue severity in prison, has
recently been investigated by the Premier, at
the instance of Mr. Maguire, M.P., who,
writing to that gentleman, says he is confirmed
in the conviction that Government would deviate
from their public duties and compromise the
interest of the community were they to admit
any claim to exceptional favour in oases snob
as those to which Mr. Maguire's letter refers.

M. Ozenue, the agent of the French Govern-
ment, has returned to Paris from London to
state the result of his negotiations with the
British Government respecting a new Commer-
cial Treaty.

An accident occurred to a Midland express
on Wednesday between Chesterfield and Shef-
field, by the breaking of the wheel of a carriage,
which threw the train off the line. None of
the passengers were injured, except one who
jumped out of the train.

A dinner has been given in New York to
Mr. J. A. Fronde, at which Mr. Bryant, Mr.
Emerson, and the Rev. Mr. Beecher were pre-
sent.

M. Maurice Richard, at whose house Prince
Napoleon was arrested, has addressed a protest
on the subject to M. Thiers. M. Richard,
passing by the illegality of the act, complains
in strong terms of the violation of his dwell-
ing, and says that had he given way to hts
indignation he should have resisted the police
by force. M. Richard furthermore expresses
regret that M. niers should forget the prin-
ciples he professed for so many years in the
Assembly, and create a dangerous precedent.

WAGES IN AUSTRALIA.

Advices from Melbourne state that the
building trades are affording full employment
to the workmen engaged in them. The wages
paid exceed those paid in the several depart-
ments in England, but the money earned does
not go so far. Stonemasons and plasterers
receive 10s. per day; carpenters from Ss. to
98 per day; slaters, 10s. to 118. per day:
bricklayers, 10s. Rer day ; labourers, from 6s.
to 7s. per day; pick and shovel men, 6s. per
day. In every instance the day's work is
calculated at eight hours. Painters and
glaziers are receiving from 9s. to 10s. per day,
While plumbers and gasfitters receive £3 per
week of eight hours per day. Coopers princi-
pally work by the piece, but for day work the
wages fixed by the trade are 10s. per day of
ten hours. Navvies on the Great Eastern
Railway are receiving 91. per hour. With
regard to other industries, we find that boiler
makers, smiths, fitters, and turners are earning
103. per day, and their labourers 7s. per day.
Competent brass finishers and copper smiths
earn from 10s. to 11s. per day; while coach
smiths receive from £2 10s. to £3 10s. per
week, and a few particularly able workmen
get as much as £4 per week. Coach body
makers, who principally work by the piece,
can earn from £3 to £3 103. Painters in this
trade receive from 9s. to lls. per day, and
trimmers from £3 to £3 103. per week. In
this trade the day's work extends over ten
hours.

Turning to mining, we fin.d that the average
rate for miners in the Ballarat district is £2
ss. per week, eight hour shifts; but brakes-
men receive slightly higher wages. In the
Bendigo district, quartz-miners in deep
sinking, for the pit work, get £2 103. ; ordinary
quartz-miners get .£2 ss. per week; engineers
receive £3 to £3 10s. In this district most
of the work is done on tribute, In Alexandria,
miners receive .£2 10s. per week. Most of
the work in Gipps' Laud is done by contract;
where wages are paid, the men receive from

The First Commissioner of Metropolitan Police,
having replied to the memorial from the men
asking more wages that he cannot, until Parliament

The undersigned, serjeants and custables of the

1. That, whereas, in the memorandum of the

for the same, while that sum is in reality very
little in excess of the daily pay of a constable, and
consequently the condition of all ranks affected by
the change, so far from being bettered, has been
made less bearable than before.

2. That while the value of money has sensibly
decreased, and the wages of the working classes
have Sustained a general advance, the salary of the
lower ranks of the polioe has become less adequate

fore made them individually less able to keep up

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 19, 1872.

LORD SALISBURY ON THE CHURCH.
LORD SALISBURY'S speech at the Church
Congress will well repay careful perusal. As
addressed to the ministers of a Church whose
members are in dangerous strife with each
other, it is precisely what might have been
expected from a clever man, and although
there is not the least chance in the world that
those to whom it was addressed will profit by
It, others who were not present, and who do
not quite agree with those who were, may
turn it to excellent account in a way not at
all contemplated by his lordship. In trying to
be a liberal churchman in the interest of the
Church, the speaker, without intending it,
did the work of a liberal man in the interest
of the nation. He put the case in such a way
as to prove more than was necessary for his
clients. In helping them forward he has
pushed them too far, and if they suffer from
his assistance they can scarcely be angry. Let
us place the several points touched on during
the speech before our readers. Lord SALIS-
BURY insisted (Ist) that the formularies of the
Church are unchangeable, because the divisions
in the Church would not permit any agree-
ment as to tho change to be made; (2nd) the
interpretation given to these by the various
parties in the Church are as wide as the
differencel which separate many perfectly
independent bodies ; (3rd) this state of things
cannot be changed, and the practical question
is, how shall we conduct ourselves under it?
(4th) we cannot call in the secular arm to
settl6 these differences, as where it has been
tried it has failed.
Here, then, are the views of the Earl of
SALISBURY, and when they are examined and
reasoned on they lead almost inevitably to
conclusions absolutely destructive to the
Church as a national institution, maintained
for the purpose of preserving and promoting
religious truth:and unity. Most sensible men
will agree with his lordship that the formu-
laries of the Church are rendered unchange-
Able, not because of their propriety or fitness,
but because the necessary agreement to change
them cannot be procured. They will also agree
to his second proposition, that the interpreta-
tion given to these by the separate parties
in the Church are as wide as the differences
which separate perfectly independent bodies.
We must not overlook, however, that a eon-
ourreue4 of opinion an thin point must lead us

to ask how that can be considered as a

national Church which is simply a number of
sects with differing beliefs and practices,
hanging together and quarrelling for no sub-
stantial reason beyond the temporal advantage
they derive by clinging to an institution
enriched by the nation's bounty ? If those
within the Church differ as much from each
other as they do from those outside, why
should they exclusively divide what, under
such circumstances, they have no exclusive
right to. Where does the central truth lie in
the institution? Which party possesses it? Is
it in one section, or does it equally enter into
the ideas of all, and if so, why is national
support denied to those ontside bodies,
hitherto excluded from the temporal ad-
vantages belonging to the national Establish-
ment?

The mere toleration by these parties of each
other, as recommended by the Marquis of
SALISBURY, would, perhaps, be decent, but it
would not be just. To agree quietly to let
each other alone and to divide in silence the
spoil, would perhaps be prudent, but it
would not justify the exclusion of others,
and if the present state of things can-
not be changed, we imagine there is a
much better method than either quietly
taking what the Church can give, or calling in
the secular arm to enforce conformity. There
can be no doubt that conformity cannot be
obtained by legal proceedings, even though
fire and faggot constituted the penalty now, as
of old. Conscientious men, who attach im-
portance to even trivial matters of doctrine and
discipline, would suffar any penalty rather
than abandon what they believe
,to be right;
whilst in the days in which we live thousands
would find a profit in being singled out for
prosecution, to say nothing'of the gratification
of personal vanity frequently found in con-
nection with such prosecutions. In fact, Lord
SALISBURY asks, as the best way of getting out
of a very grave difficulty, that all sectional '
differences should be tolerated in the Church
rather than resort to the secular arm; but to
compensate for this he would not on any
account allow what he calls personal eccen-
tricities. If men differ in 'groups ho would
allow them to do so, but if they differed singly
he would permit the bishop to lay on the tem-
poral lash. Regard this as we may, it simply
means that any number of creeds or any
variety of practices may be tolerated if indi-
vidual crotchets and eccentricities are kept in
check. What this would lead to it is not diffi-
cult to guess. But then the difficulty of the
other alternative is no loss perplexing. For
the dominant party to drive the others out,
even by the help of the State, would certainly
be a hopeless task, to say nothing of the
damaging scandal such a proceeding would
bring upon the Church. If the bishops could
even succeed in performing so hopeless a task,
the Church would no longer be the Church of
the nation; the little it has of strength, of en--
thusiasm, of popular affection would pass
away from it, and leave it stripped of every-
thing that can give it any claim to continue
its existence as a national institution.

The scene at the Leeds Congress whilst the
various speakers wore dealing with the im-
portant question as to the "first principle of

the Church's comprehensiveness in *matters of
doctrine and ritual," clearly displayed the
bigotry and intolerance of the spirit at present
existing in the Establishment. The reporters
of the newspaper press describe the Town
Hall, whilst a good part of the discussion went
on, as a "bear garden," and from the speci-
mens given, the expression does not appear
too strong. The divisions existing, however
they may appear to the public mind, are
marked and decided in the minds of the clergy
and their most zealous followers ; so marked
and decided as to leave no chance of recon-
cilement, and little hope of unity of doctrine
and practice being again restored in the
Church. In fact, it shows the utter useless-
ness of an effort recently meditated of bring-
ing the various bodies of Protestant dissenters
back into the fold of the Mother Church, as
instead of reconciling differences in a spirit of
charity they are multiplying parties in a
spirit of strife. They have Thirty-nine
Articles not to believe in, but to sign and to
fight about. Those oonatituto the maximum

of a belief, the minimum of which would be
difficult to ascertain. There is beside the
Athanasian Creed, which is an abomination
to some ; an affliction ,to all. There is a
Prayer-book to be reformed, a ritual to be
regulated. There is, in fact, everything
necessary to set the ministers and members of
the Church at strife, and to turn their attempts
at deliberation into scenes befitting a "bear
garden."
There is one effectual cure. If they eannot
agree in the Church, and won't leave it, let
them be turned out to take their chance in the
world as other respectable believers do. We
had better have no established Church than
one which seems to be employed chiefly as a
forcing bed for schism. Let the Evangelicals,
the Ritualists, and all others sot themselves up
in their own way, and promulgate their special
views at their own expense. When separated
from each other, and with no spoil to light
about, they will agree just as all other sects
do. An united Church teaching a truth upon
which all its ministers are agreed is one
thing; a divided Church with a disputed
truth and an irreconcilable method of teach-
ing is something very different. The one may
rest for support on public utility; the other
can have no such pretension.

Time was when Governments wanted such
aid as the priests of an establisled religion
could give—the necessity for this has now
nearly disappeared. The multiplication and
subdivision of sects has almost entirely neutra-
lized the dangerous power once possessed by
an established Church in England. The poli-
tical thought of the nation is not now in the
keeping of the Chnrch. Nay, its own thought
has got beyond its own control. To disestab-
lish and disendow it would be to cause its dis-
integration, and by so doing give rival
activities and zeals separate fields of &Alen
in which they could labour peaceably and use-
fully for the promotion of religion. Where
the ministers could draw from their followers
the cost of their work, leaving to the nation
for the promotion of national objects, revenues
which at present do not realize the meaning
and intention of the past, nor promise in any
proper way to further the highest hopes of
men in regard to the world's future.

THE PALMERSTONIAN CANDIDATE
FOR TIVERTON.

No member of Parliament in our time was
more popular with his constitutents than was
Lord PALMERSTON. He possessed a captivating
manner, which it was his uniform habit every-
where and in all circumstances to display.
Even now, we suppose, nobody could offer
himself to the electors of Tiverton more
acceptably than as a former follower of that
accomplished chief. Mr. MASSEY has this
advantage, with some recommendations be.
longing to himself. His candidature in
Devonshire is, however, less interesting with
reference to the question whether this Western
borough will choose an avowed PALMERSTONIAN
or a Conservative of Mr. WuatoNn's
class, than as that of a man who, having
served in former Parliaments under the
Neill() Viscount, withdrew from the stage,
accepting an appointment which introduced
him to Eastern life, and, on his return home,
has remained for a while a passive observer of
the GLADSTONIAN, as succeeding to the PAL-
XERSTONIAN, system of things. Moreover,
those historical studies and labours with.which
Mr. MASSEY illustrated a portion of his period
of retirement from active polities, may be sup-
posed to have fed and confirmed those of
his views on public( questions, legislation and
government, which have grown up in his mind
independent of any,master or leader in polemical
politics.

For example; he was honestly able to open
his mouth at Tiverton, with the declaration,
that, having always supported the Ballot when
he sat in the House of Commons, he congra-
tulated the electors, many of whom are
.outside
the town, upon now proceeding to a fresh
choice under the protection of a secret vote.
He is equally sound with respect to what
those who style themselves "Conservatives "
are so much in love with, the cumulative vote.
In his judgment, they knew not what they
did when they endeavoured to load household
suffrage with that clog. It would have set up

an odious distinction between rich and poor, in
the union of whom all are interested, but none
so deeply as those who wish what are called
the "rights of property" to be altered,
weakened, or disturbed as little as possible.
In one modern discovery made by party perspi-
cacity, OUT revived PALMERSTONIAN has not a
particle of faith. To him the vaunted "Con-
servative working man" is either a miracle of
easy faith or "the meanest of sneaks," if not
a myth of fancy. This, at least, is throwing
down the glove to opponents; for, if such an
order of beings any where exists, a Devonshire
borough enlarged from the adjacent Hundreds,
should be the stage on which they might be
most effectively produced.
_ _

Those meditative habits which a olever and
aging man may be supposed to have cultivated
during a retreat of years from the arena of
contending parties have not prevented Mr.
MASSEY from daring the Tories of Devon to
do their utmost to send him back to his retire-
ment. The party, he scornfully avers, havo
not a rag of principle to clothe their nakedness
withal. They can no longer torment Roman
Catholics, or oppress Protestant Dissenters.
The questions that constituted their political
life are dead and buried. GLADSTONE is Dives,
and they are the dogs fain to prolong a hungry
existence on the crumbs that fall from the
Rich Man's table. The Liberals, on the con-
trary, sit round a board of plenty in a house.
hold where the hired servants have bread enough
and to spare. Whether or not the candidate
for Tiverton is to return to that happy family
in the character of the Prodigal Son we do not
profess to know.

He seems, at any rate, to have a shrewd
guess of what is about to be put on the table.
In the year 1873, he says, the Liberals will
bring to bear the same courage and earnest-
ness as in the past. Financial questions de-
mand earnest consideration, and be hopes to
see our whole fiscal system submitted to scien-
tific revision, so that burdens on different
classes may be equitably adjusted. The in-
come tax presses severely on trades and pro-
fessions, and requires considerable amendment.
Important changes in land laws are impend-
ing; in the interest of property he desires to
see laws regulating the transmission and en-
joyment of land receive the earliest attention
of the Government. As to the game laws, lie
likes legitimate sport, but to have hecatombs
of hares, rabbits, and pheasants driven up to
an armoury of guns is not sport but slaughter.
The higher classes are exceedingly ill-advised
to pursue sport in that extravagant and ab-
surd manner. So far as he had power he
would not suffer the material interests of the
country to be sacrificed to the amusements of
any class.

Mr. MAssEr, on the whole, leaves it inde-
terminate whether he seeks a seat as an inde-
pendent man, or as a candidate for a slice of
the fatted calf. Charged with being "a fol-
lower of Mr. GLADSTONE," he does not exactly
repel the imputation, but he significantly
claims to be "an older Reformer than he."
Besides, Mr. GLADSTONE'S opinions have
"undergone changes," although "at least, he
believed, settled down into sincere, enlightened,
and ardent attachment to civil and religious
liberty:" whereas Mr. MASSEY is what he has
always been. At any rate, he will be no man's
slave, GLADSTONE or any other, but "claims
the right acquired by long Parliamentary ex-
perience and varied knowledge of public life to
exercise and express an independent opinion."
It is curious, therefore, that, while viewing
the PREMIER in the light of a recent convert to

Liberal opinions, he -should seem to single out
MT. FORSTER as the man in the Ministry after
his own heart. The VICE-PRESIDENT is "an
honourable Minister ; " and he "admires the
honesty of purpose and of policy with which
he handled the education question." True,
the Act is not so complete as it might have
been, had the framer been "left to his
unbiassed will." Particular features require
revision; but Mr. MISSEY will pledge himself
on none of them, "being desirous not to

embarrass the Right Honourable gentleman."
In short, Mr. llkssEY evidently looks forward
to something that he either wishes or expects.
In a special address to the outlying voters,
some of whom may be labourers, but princi-
pally farmers, he was all upon the Lan&

Question. In future, he said, the attention
of the country, and especially of the Liberals,
who would always be the governing party,
would be directed chiefly to agricultural
questions. Farmers had many grievances, and
bad a right to complain. The evils were of
artificial creation, caused by laws which had
become antiquated. The law which kept land
in the possession of great families by a series
of artificial successions was of this character.
Such laws might suit England when half-
populated; but the country was now swarm-
ing with 'people. The increase of population
compelled a relaxation of laws, considered
thirty years ago absolutely necessary. All
ether land reforms are trifling compared with
the laws restricting transmission of land.
These were invented to maintain the aristo-
cracy. With no desire to subvert the
_aristo-
cracy, Mr. MASSEY does desire reforms which
many of that class may think unfriendly to
them, but which are demanded by the interests
of the community. The enormous cost at-
tending the transmission of land has been
somewhat mitigated. That was an admission
of the principle, which must be pushed to its
full extent, until land is transferred as easy as
horses. The tenant, moreover, ought not to be
liable to have his rent raised because of im-
provements effected by his own capital, nor
should he be capriciously dismissed. Such is
Mr. MASSEY'S view as to the way the wind is
blowing.

A VERY interesting series of articles is now
in course of publication in the Daily News on
the condition of the miners in various parts of
the country. These articles are sufficiently
graphic) and picturesque, and in their general
outline true enough, in regard to the actual life
of the people. In these descriptions, allusion
is frequently made to the improvident habits
of the miner. Ho drinks his money when he
ought to reserve it for better purposes. lie
Over-eats himself. He gets drunk. He
indulges in dogs, and the amusements carried
on by Means of that sagacious creature. Ile, in
fact, wastes his time in many ways, and leaves
his children without education, or regular and
proper food, and his cottage without even the
simplest means of decent accommodation.
Something of a like kind is said of the
agricultural labourers by country gentlemen
and members of Parliament. He, too, has a
weakn.ess for beer, and wastes the money
Which ought to be spent at home at the
public-house or beershop. The other higher
luxuries of occasional gorging and dog-fancy-
ing he is debarred froni by want of means.
We do not condemn this kind of writing
for want of truth. Unhappily it is too true,
and if it could be cured by a universal ex-
izession of public indignation, we should be
delighted if it was poured hotly upon all such
Offenders from every point of the compass.
If there is a sight between heaven and earth
calculated to make a man despair of his
follow-creatures, it is that of working men
spending their means in brutalizing dissipa-
tion, to the neglect of their families, and con-
firming a race of degraded brutalized slaves,
without mind, heart, decency, ambition, or
hope.

It would be as well, however, if, in criti-
cising this state of things WQ mixed some
degree of pity with our indignation against
these slaves of ignorance and vice, and also
some degree of shame against ourselves for
permitting such an evil state Of things to
continue with the means in our hands to put
a stop to it. Children born ia cottages with-
out furniture, brought up in filth and igno-
rance, who draw their breath in fetid vapours,
to Whom cleanliness is almost an impossibility,
who hear no language that is not a mixture
of gutter vulgarity, ribaldry, and profaneness,
are not likely to be gentlemen and ladies
when they arrive at maturity, And it may be
added that when such a state of things is
allowed to come into existence, it never car-
ries in it the power of self-cure. Nor is it in
accordance with Christianity, or even with a
decent heathenism, that it should be aban-
doned to its own -unaided efforts.

When we read the horrors published by the
Daily NOWS WO know that the description does
not refer to any sayage tribe in the unexplored

wilds of the world, nor even to those
savages who, though wild, and uncivilized,
have still in them a touch of the original
dignity of manhood, a bright trace of the finger
of GOD. Our mining savages, such as they
have been described, are blurred all over with
the pawing of the Devil, and this with arch-
bishops, and bishops, and rectors, and all else
paid for by the nation, that SITIN may be
combatted in his foulest strongholds, and
Englishmen, women, and children rescued
from his horrible grasp. Have we not also
great missionary societies busy everywhere
amongst far-off heathens, active amongst
Jews? And besides all this, have we not
wealthy and respectable men in the nation ?
men whose possessions have become the
wonder and envy of the world, obtained
through the industry of these poor, blurred,
half-brutal men? And though last, not least,
have we not a newspaper press which pene-
trates everywhere, whose influence for good
or evil is unbounded, yet whose cue it is
to praise and not to reproach those who per-
mit these festering social sores to continue,
who allow thorn to' spread and deepen under
their noses without any effort worth speaking
of to cure them or cut them:out. Such filthy
spots as Dowlais, and there are many of them
throughout this favoured land, are disgraceful
no doubt to those who inhabit them; but they
are also disgraceful to the press, which could
make employers and proprietors a bye-word
for the world. if they did not attend to thorn,
and see to their (lure. These papers can make
us see with shame the want of decency by
which such places are characterized, but
they take no trouble to point out the lack of
justice and the absence of duty by which they
come into existence, and are allowed to con-
tinue. These are hidden, not exposed, and
the other abominations would also be hidden
did not the newspapers, &using the slack
season, need a little picturesque and sensa-
tional writing to stimulate circulation. The
over-abundant beer of the ignorant squalid
working brute is paraded before the reader;
but not a word of the thousand indulgences
by which the rich squander means which if
rightly applied would soon sweeten such
abominations as Dowlais. Let us have fair
play all round, and whilst we lash heartily
such sins as those committed by the colliers of
Dowlais, let us not forget the guilty backs of
those who claim the profit made g such places,
without acknowledging or fulfilling the duties
implied by the connection which brings them
that profit.

EMPLOYMENT OF SOLDIERS IN HAR-
VESTING.

WE are not desirous to press anything un-
duly against the Government, but as we were
the first to call public attention to the hiring
out of soldiers to work in the harvest fields,
we shall feel it our duty to press the question
until the Government has given the country
the fullest assurance that such an act in hos-
tility to the interest of the labourers shall not
be repeated. We are willing to take Mr.
GLIDSTONE'S assurance, given through his
secretary to Mr. BINIIS, that the matter is now
"undergoing careful examination,'' and we
shall very patiently await the result of that
examination. But no examination can alter
the fact, which seems to be beyond all dispute
or cavil, that the soldiers were sent into the
harvest field and did work for the farmers,
which the labourers were quite willing to do
at a fair price, and thus, by competing
against the labourers in the interest of the
farmers, the families of these poor men were
deprived of their ordinary means of support.
We know before hand the kind of defence
that will be set up—excuses for such a pro-
ceeding lie about abundantly enough. But
the Government and the War Office authori-
ties may as well at once understand that
they will not be accepted as justifications by
working men. We do not wish to see Govern-
ment stores, or our Cavalry horses, or any-
thing belonging to the public, put into the
market at a particular moment to compete
with dealers of any kind for the purpose of
keeping down prices. And we shall certainly
not stand silently by if the resources of the
army or navy are used for the purpose of beat-
ing down or keeping down wages. If this
preeeoding
iniquitous should Jae. repeated,

every working man in the country will practi-
cally and firmly protest against the Govern-
ment that permits it. The most devoted Con.
servative working man, touched by such a
wrong, Nvuld become indignant, as even with
them there must be a point where a sense of
justice and fairness outraged would rouse
them to action.

If this act is not utterly repudiated Mr.
CARD WELL'S scheme for teaching soldiers
certain handicraft trades, presumed to be
useful to the service, must be opposed to the
uttermost. Every trades society in England,
and every trade net in union, must make this
a common cause, and at every election any
candidate that countenances such a:proceeding
must in the interest of labour be rejected.
To return candidates is a much more difficult
thing than to prevent theta from being
returned, and the working men in any borough
or city in the kingdom—nay, in many of the
counties—could send to the right-about any
man who gave countenance to such a Dais— '
chievous unfairness. Working men are, no
doubt, ignorant in multitudes of instances,
blind and stupid in Many respects, much dis-
posed to play the flunkey in the presence of
titled and wealthy mediocrity. But our
Government and our military authorities
may rest assured they are not quite so
ignorant, so blind, or so stupid as to allow the
bread to be taken out of their children's
mouths by the employment of soldiers in com-
petition with themselves for the advantage of
employers either ia our fields or our work-
shops.
MR. MASSEY AT TIVERTON.

Mn. MASSEY, the Liberal candidate for
Tiverton, addressing a meeting of the electors,
said a Conservative working man was "either
an embodiment of most exalted Christian
charity, or else the meanest sneak that could
disgrace the class to which he belonged." So
far as it goes this is correct, but it excludes
the largest portion of those who delight to call
themselves "operative Conservatives." There
may be a few in the first category, but, we
suspect, not many. Men who, by experience,
or by reading, understand the past, who,
therefore, know something of the evil done by
the Conservative party in obstructing reforms
necessary for the well-being of those who live
by their labour, and who, knowing this, pos-
sess Christian charity enough to forgive those
from whom they have suffered injury, are but
few. There is, however, the other class. The
"sneaks" who, being cheated and kicked,
honour the superior intelligence by which they
have been swindled, o.nd are prepared to kiss
the toe by which they have been assaulted in
the rear. Unhappily there are too many. of
these. They have no sense of what is due to
them or their class, and by the mere lowness
of their natures, spaniel like, they lick the
hand that smites them. Bat the true expla-
nation of what is called the existence of opera-

tive Conservatism is neither an abnormal
charity or meanness, but a stupidity, which
though provoking and humiliating enough,
yet is not, either very exalting or depressing.
Amongst the working men we have some of
the most intelligent and liberal of our politi-
cians, but we have also a large number of per-
sons who, by mere ignorance, by an utter
absenceof ideas, are led away in any direction
the passion or prejudice of the moment may
point out ; and it [must be confessed that Mr.
MASSEY'S political friends have acted in such
a manner as to try the loyalty of men not be-
longing to the mere ignorant portion of their
own party. We have, it is true, a right to
look for good sense amongst working men,
and a sufficient understanding of what is due
to them from the Legislature. But it is, also,
our duty to demand from the chiefs of the
Liberal party a policy so sound and liberal as
to secure every man belonging to the party
whose support is worth having.

LABOUR AGENCY-FOREIGN WORK-
MEN.

WE publish in another column the circular
of Mr. J. H. DUDGEON, dated from 6.1, Austin
Friars, that our worliing readers may under-
stand the kind of influences they have to con-
tend against, Mr. DUDGEON is troubled by
"the growing power of the working classes,"
and he calls for a " Labour Agency" for the
purpose of counteracting this power. We have
no objection to this; we acknowledge the
right of the employers to set up such an agency,
though we regard the objects stated as utterly
chimerical. They cannot bring men here
from the Continent when they want
them in such numbers and of such a character
as they require. Besides, there is nothing they
can do in this way which English working men
cannot counteract by a little trouble, and the
expenditure of an amount of money quite
moderato compared to what it will cost em-
ployers to keep such a machinery as that pro-
posed by Mr. DUDGEON in motion. We do
not, however, by any means desire to discourage
Mr. DUDGEON'S proposal; on the contrary, we
should very much like to see the employers in
every branch of business go into association for
the purpose of doing jointly whatever may
seem best for the promotion of their true in-
terests. We are satisfied that much of the
intemperate folly by which their proceedings
against the men in their employment is cha-
racterized is due to their habit of acting
separately and apart from each other. Closer
assooiation and a more intimate acquaintance
with each other's proceedings would teach them
that their best interest is to be found in their
agreement with their men, and that however
valuable men may be who are brought from
the Continent or elsewhere, the most valuable
man in England, as a workman, is the English-
man, who has been born and brought up in the
country—or, as SITIXESPEARE says—" Whose
bones were made in England," and whose alle-
giance and loyalty are native here as well as
the employment by which he lives.
Were the employers together in association
they would soon find this out, notwithstanding
the " Cosmopolitan " tendencies of Mr. DUD-
GEON, and this discovery would lead them to
seek for friendly and kindly relationships with
their men in a way that would be profitable to
both parties. The workshops of England filled
with the waifs and strays of the Continent,
with, perhaps, contingents of coolies, with the
DUDGEONS at the top as " bosses " appointed
by Providence, would hardly be an improve-
ment on the present state of things, ugly as it
may look in the eyes of gentlemen whose
minds are filled with trouble because they can-
not have everything their own way.

articles.title: FIRE AT MR. MITCHELL'S MARBLE WORKS.
articles.text:
FIRE AT MR. MITCHELL'S MARBLE
WORKS.

The Builder of Saturday, referring to the fire
which we noticed last week, says :—Most of our
readers will have heard of the great fire which
took place, at 148, Upper Thames-street, on Friday
evening in last week, whereby nearly the whole
of Mr. Mitchell's valuable stock of marble
mantelpieces, stoves, and sculptured work has been
totally destroyed. Although Mr. Mitchell has in
consequence lost property to the extent of between
£5,000 and £6,000, which 1.3 only partly insured,
we are happy to say that the loss is not ruinous.
The circumstance of this fire is only one more
striking incident in a very singular career. From
a book which has recently been published, "The
Romance of Peasant Life in the West of E
by Francis G-eorge Health, we learn that about 28
years ago Mr. Mitchell was a poor farmyard boy
in Somersetshire, earning 4s. a week in the employ
of a hard and cruel master. He possessed, how-
ever, a singular amount of energy and persever-
ance. At 19 years of age ho left his native
village—Montacute, near Yeovil—and although
he could not read or write, he came to London.
He had previously picked up some knowledge of

tlie stonomasou'd trade. We extract the follow-
ing from the book to
_which we have referred:—

The remainder of George Mitchell's career may
be told in a few words. During the 25 years
that he has been in London he has exhibited a
truly remarkable amount of perseverance and
ability in the prosecution of his business. From
step to step he slowly and surely advanced. From
a mason's lad he became a journeyman; and from
a journeyman a small proprietor; and from the
position of the small proprietor he advanced to
that of the rich and prosperous merchant; and 1
am assured that at the present time his business
is one of themost prosperous ot its kind in England.
"But," said Mr. Mitchell to me, "in my great
prosperity I have not forgotten my former condition
in life. My heart bleeds for the poor farm
labourers in my native village, and I have told
them that if the farmers will not better their con-
dition, I will guarantee to find employment for a
number of them in connection with my own trade
in London.'"

Mr. Mitchell has taken a wry active part in the
agricultural labourers' movement, and his time
and his money have been expended upon the cause.
We are glad to know that the present loss will not
in any way interfere with his business. The
Upper Thames-street branch is now being tem-
porarily carried on at 1, Duck's-foot-lane; his
show-rooms in the Brompton-road are full of
stock; and his works in Walton-street, Brompton,
are in full activity.

articles.title: DISESTABLISHMENT.
articles.text:
DISESTABLISHMENT.

The Manchester Guardian makes the following
comment on the meeting lately held in the Free
Trade Hall :—Mr. Miall has been solemnly de-
posed from his rank as agitator in chief against
the National Church. The pre-eminence has been
wrested from him by a professional lecturer. On
Tuesday night Mr. Mason Jones informed those
who are at all interested in the matter that "he
was at issue" with Mr. Miall and the Birmingham
Conference as to the political action which should
be taken to hasten the overthrow of the Church.
He thinks the member for Bradford and Mr. Dale
too slow—cautious old fogies who must be set aside
if the work is to go merrily on. 110 is for action
at all hazards, and excited Liberationists must
ponder regretfully over a fact proclaimed on the
authority of Mr. Jones himself that the question
would at this moment have been in "a more ad-
vaneed position" if he (Mr. Jones) had not, unfor-
tunately, been laid aside by feeble health during
the last year and a half. Greater things may now
be expected. It says well for Mr. Jones's physical
condition that he was able to deliver himself of a
two hours' "oration" on Tuesday night, and be
tells us that he means serious business. The Free
Trade Hall meeting, he declared, "inaugurated a
new epoch in English political life." The Bir-
mingham Conference was nothing, or at the most
a mere gathering of timid wavering temporizers,
who either did not know, or were wanting in the
courage required, to proceed at once to the attack.
The man, as well as the hour, has now come.
Mr. Jones has commenced a struggle "tremendous
in its issues, and one the magnitude of which had
not been surpassed by any during the last two
centuries." " Cowards, timid people, and trim-
mers"—the members of the Birmingham Confer-
ence, we presume—are warned to stand aside.
Where hot work is to be done, men of different
meal() IIN WAnted. llii Appeg ie to "the great-

mass of the English people." Victory, it need not
be said, is assured; who can doubt that ? Jones
leads, and all England will, of course, follow in a
frenzy of enthusiasm. The bishops had better
pack up at once.

articles.title: MINERS' RIGHT TO VOTE.
articles.text:
THE MINERS' RIGHT TO VOTE.

At the 31orpeth Borough Revision Court, on
Monday, before Mr. Trevelyan, miners' claims
were considered. These numbered above 2,000,
and are in the townships of Blythe, Bedlington,
Newsham, Bebside, and other outlying districts
of the extensive borough of Morpeth. In some
cases it was shown that the colliery regulatiors
as to the occupancy of cottages declared that the
occupants should not be deemed tenants, and the
Revising Barrister unhesitatingly declared that
these men Were simply servants, and could not
sustain their claims. In another class of cases no
such agreement or regulation existed, and these
occupiers were held to be entitled to vote, but
inasmuch as the tenants were not on the rate-
book, and had not claimed to have their names
placed there, they could not be put on the
register. On this point, however, he offered to
grant a case, seeing that the claimants contended
it was not necessary to claim to be on the rate-
book, or even to be upon it, but that it was the
duty of the overseers to put the names there;
any omission, however, not invalidating the
claimants' right to vote. The court adjourned till
Tuesday for evidence as to other collieries, but the
result practically is that the Revising Barrister
has decided against all the claims.

articles.text:
REVIEWS.

CASSELL'S TECHNICAL SERIES.

When the wealthy capitalists of this coun-
try first began to _discover that the manufac-
turers of the Continent of Europe were
treading close upon their heels in certain
classes of production, they naturally sought the
cause of, what some had said, was our decline
in the markets of the world.

"It must be these strikes that are driving
trade away from the country," said the quid-
nunes, and so the cry was repeated, parrot-
like, all over the country. " Not so,'' an-
swered the trades union leaders, "if we are
being beaten, which we deny, the cause is not
far to seek—our education,has been negleeted ;
whilst Peussia, Saxony, Belgium, France, and
other places are seeking to develop° the skill
of their artizans, England, with glorious free-
dom, leaves her workmen to shift for them-
selves."

Farther inquiries diligantly sot on foot by

the Government, tom us too plainly that in
certain industries the goods were being
"turned out better" by reason of the tech-
nical education of those engaged in the work.
We must educate was then the cry, and real
earnest efforts are now being made to secure
for our workmen that efficiency and skill which
increased education can alone give.
But we are a slow people, and many years
must elapse before our boys can become edu-
cated workmen.

Meanwhile, manuals are being published
suitable both for schools and self-instruction,
and first in the list we must name " Cassell's
Technical Series." The mere mention of the

names of those already published would be too

tedious for a notice of this character, but
the series nommences with "Linear Draw-

ing " and "Projeotion," and takes the student
through a complete course of scientific in-
struction, forming a basis upon which to raise
a superstructure suitable to the special
requirements of the learner, or the more ad-
vanced mechanic,

It too often happened in the past that a
7 bully" became a foreman, not in consequence
' of his skill, but because of his aptitude for
" driving ;" and frequently have we known a
more skilled workman kept as a kind of " Man
Friday," to read and lay out all the plans,
and even keep the time-sheets and accounts.
But that day is fast passing away, and the
" bully" will no longer be able to hold his
own amongst well-educated and skilful work-
men. Our advice, therefore, to all those whose
education has been neglected in youth, is to
spend, a few shillings in " Cassell's Technical
Series," beginning with "Linear Drawing"
and "Projection "—two volumes in one, price
as. 6d. Then to follow these up with "Build-
ing Construction and Architeetural Drawing,"
' and so on, through such volumes of the series
as best meet his own • requirements in the
, special trade to which he belongs. An earnest
application during the winter months would
soon repay the student for all the time, money,.
and care which he had expended in purchasing
and mastering the valuable information con-
tained in these volumes.

THREE GOOD SHIPS.
Three good shipscerne sailing. in,

Long ago, ay, long ago—
Three good ships came sailing in
So early in the morning,
And all the winds to th' shore did blow,
And all the sails were as white as snow,

So early in the morning.
Three good ships so brave and new,
Long ago, ay, long ago,
Three good ships so brave and now,
Early in the morning,
And th' sea was smooth and the sky was blue,
And every soul on board was true,
Early in the morning.
Sailing over the silver sea,
Long ago, ay-, long ago
Freighted with freight that was all for me
Early in the morning,
And "hope" and "Faith," they were stout and

tall,
But "Love" was the best ship of them all,
Early in the morning.
Three good ships a-sailing in,
Long ago, ay, long ago,
Three good ships a-sailing in
Early in the morning;
But there were breakers to be crossed,
And one of the three good ships was lost,
Early in the morning.
Two good ships a-sailing in,
Slow and sad and sad and slow,
Two good ships a-sailing in
Through the cloudy morning;
For air and sky were all a-frown,
And of the two ships one went down,
In the mournful morning.

Sailing over the solemn sea,
Through the foam, th' °old white foam,
One good ship is left to me
Far away from the morning;
Hope and Love they both are gone,
But Faith is sailing sadly on
Towards the eternal morning.

A. C.

articles.title: SOULPTOR'S TRIUMPH.*
articles.text:
THE SOULPTOR'S TRIUMPH.*

In the palmiest days of art in Florence, one of
its grand Dukes made known by proclamation
that he designed to add to the statues which
adorned his palace, a representation of Mary, the
pardoned sinner, anointing the Saviour's feet,
which she had washed with her penitent tears, and
wiped with flowing hair. The space of one year'
was allowed for the creation of a chef d'ecurre.
Three venerable sculptors were appointed as judges.
At the expiration of the allotted time, they were
commissioned to visit the atelier of every artist
who notified them that he had a Mary to offer, and
decide what statues were worthy of being sent to
the ducal palace for further examination. There
the final selection was to be made by thirty-four
judges. The sculptor whose chisel produced a
marble Mary of superlative beauty, was to receive
the sum of £5OO for his labour. But mere gold
mattered little, compared •to the honour of a
triumph which opened a brilliant career to the
successful aspirant.
Need we number the artists who were com
petitors for the invaluable distinction P
The day previous to the one fixed for the ex-
hibition arrived—the day upon which the three
judges made their rounds, and awarded permission
for the statues approved to enter the palace on
the morrow.

Many a heart in Florence grew sick with
alternations of hope and fear, Many an artist's
soul was filled with despair as he recognized the
vast distance that existed between his actual exe-
cution and the sublime heights reached by his
Ideal conception. Many others, gifted with the
gigantic self-esteem which is often the blemish of
genius, exulted in the certainty of their triumph,
and unrebuked by a doubt of their own surpassing
merits, impatiently awaited the coming of the
judges.
In one studio sat a youth who had seen the
roses of but twenty-two summers bloom and
wither. Though the dawn had scarcely broken he
was dressed with scrupulous care, and his pictu-
resque attire of black velvet displayed to advantage
his lithely moulded form, and imparted a striking
transparency to his colourless complexion. His
hollow cheeks bespoke vigils of study and labour;
his dark, deeply sunken eyes, full of restless fire,
betrayed a fervid and highly sensitive organization
—a temperament at once Imaginative and volcanic.
His hair, of purple blackness, wandered in un-
taught curls from beneath a velvet cap, shading
his expansive brow, and eloquent, though too
sharply cut, features.
His studio was somewhat bare. A crimson
curtain divided the apartment. As the golden rays
of morning began to illumine the chamber, Andrea
was roused from his reverie. He rose and bolted
the door—a precaution always taken before that
curtain was thrown aside. Now, with eager
movements, be flung back the crimson folds and
again sank into his seat. As he contemplated the
treasure disclosed, what rapidly varying expres-
SLUM chased each other over his countenance, like
a changing panorama fitfully reflected in some
pellucid mirror.
Before him stood a marble wonder, indeed!
The plaster model was partially visible in the back
;pound. In general, sculptors do not themselves
handle the chisel except to give a few finishing

• The leading incident of this narrative has been used
in a Freneb, dregia, entitled, "Le Chef 4,cettyr,

and embellishing touches. The laborious, me-
chanical duty of copying in marble, by close
measuremeut from the plaster cast, is usually
entrusted to skilful workmen; but Andrea felt as
though his exquisite creation would have been
profaned if other eyes rested upon it, other hands
touched it during its incompletion. He had called
his Mary into existence out of the snowy block
himself. Truth to say, he had manipulated as
lightly and tenderly as though he feared the frigid
stone were gifted with sensation, as though he
thought each moment that it would pulsate with
life. Pygmalion looked not more enamoured of the
loveliness that bad started into shape beneath his
touch than the young, unnoted, Florentine sculptor
in the presence of the, Mary he had evoked!
It was a gloriously beautiful form, full of the
most exquisite delicacy, the most speaking grace,
the most touching purity. The kneeling figure,
though ethereally ft ivgile, was rounded to such
perfection that laughing dimples were pressed
upon the falling shoulders, the Andalusian feet,
the dainty hands. These were bare, and the
swell of the expanding bosom, just budding into
the fulness of womanhood, was revealed beneath
the transparent drapery. The small poetically
shaped head was raised, disclosing the graceful
curve of the slender throat ;--the upturned face
seemed gazing with inspired devotion, into that of
the Saviour. The hair flowed to the ground in
rippling waves. One hand held the box of oint-
ment; the other clasped the clustering tresses, as
though in the act of pressing them upon the
Redeemer's feet.
But there was a marked defect in the marble
representation, though Andrea saw it not. That
face and form inspired the gazer with a sense of
the spiritualizing power of perfect chastity. Its
loveliness was that of the most unsullied inno-
cence. No trace of sensuous emotion was visible.
it was not possible to imagine that one, whose
soul had been heavy with sin, could ever again
wear a look so pure.
While Andrea sat dreaming before his master-
piece, a light tap on the door was thrice repeated,
as though for a signal. Andrea started up, and
his pale countenence flushed with a sudden glow
of rapture. Is it the judges he is expecting, so
soon after the sunrise? The bolt is rapidly with-
drawn—the door opens—a young girl, followed
by a sort of nurse, or gouvornante, enters.
" Constanza, 3,'ou have eonie!"
"Did I ever fail you, Andrea?"

"Never, my gad angel, my saint of Inspira-
tion! Come, and let me see if I can dare to look
once more upon the copy, and behold it fade into
dull, intpotent insignificance before the divine
original !"
Andrea's Mary was not the offspring of his
imagination—there, before him, beamed that
guileless countenance, stood that shape full of
artless grace and infantile purity, which he had
so faithfully transmitted to marble. But the
"lunar beauty of sculpture" could not convey the
lustre of those clear, blue eyes, the amber gleam-
ing of the hair—the peach-like hue of the cheeks,
the dewy rosiness of the tender lips, the auroral
freshness of the whole form.

Something more than two years previous to the
date of our narrative, her father chanced to see a
statuette of St. Catherine modelled by Andrea,
and was struck by the genius evinced by its execu-
tion. The Duke was not only an experienced judge
but a liberal patron of art. lie at once purchased
the St. Catharine, sought out the young sculptor,
and engaged him to adorn a hall of his palace
with bas reliefs.

• _
A room was appropriated to Andrea's use, for
the prosecution of his work. The Duke and his
daughter watched its progress with deep interest.
Indeed, Constanza, when her studies were accom-
plished, daily wandered to the apartment where
the young sculptor was employed. That one as
sensitive to physical beauty as Andrea, finding it
united to rare mental loveliness, should have
become enamoured of this paragon of maidenhood,
was almost a matter of course. But Andrea wor-
shipped in respectful silence, and never had the
audacity to suppose that his passion had revealed
itself in his looks, never dared to hope that she
who inspired it could become conscious of its
existence—never was mad enough to dream for a
moment that, if divined, it could ever be re-
turned.

The bas reliefs completed, the sculptor with-
drew, full of gratitude to his noble patron, and
bearing, with him the image of Constanza, in-
delibly stamped on his own soul! She was the far-
off star that henceforth illumined his horizon,
though deemed as unapproachable by him as con-
stellations are to mortals.
What was his astonishment when Oonstanza,
with her faithful attendant, Bertina, who had
watched over the motherless young maiden from
her infancy, made their appearance at his atelier!
They came again and again; and Constanza, un-
conscious as Desdemona of the betrayal of her
affection, like Desdemona, was "half the wooer."
Andrea's discretion was put to flight—in an
unguarded moment he poured forth his hopeless
passion—asking and expecting nothing but the
privilege of saying that he loved and despair ed-,
the joy of daring to believe that his love was not
spurned. To aspire to the hand of a Florentine
lady of high lineage, fleetned too wild a vision
oven for an enthusiast. But the gentle Oonstanza
thought otherwise.

"You will be famous one of these days," she
timidly said; "you will win renown equal to that
of Michael • Angelo, and than my father will not
refuse you his child. Genius has a nobility of its
own, far higher and worthier than that of acci-
dental descent. We have only to wait—wait for
years perhaps—many years! Wait until clustering
laurels have crowned your brow, and then you
may place the bridal chaplet upon mine."
So she prattled on in her hopeful, innocent way,
and Andrea, against his better judgment, could
not forego the happiness of believing her words.
When the prize for a Mary wee offered by the
Grand Duke, Andrea immediately became one of
the competitors. Was it wonderful that he un—
emulously communicated to his design the fge

and form over present to his mind? Old Bettina
first discovered the resemblance. Then Constanza
impulsively proposed to sit as the model for her
lover. How could he refuse? Day after day,
before the house was astir, she and Bettina stole
forth, under the pretence of taking a morning
walk, and hastened to Andrea's studio. All the
young artist's faculties were quickened by love
and ambition. All his powers in the fulness of
their strength, were concentrated on this one work
—the chef d'ffluvre which was to earn him fame
and win the bright original he was duplicating.
"Are you content with your Mary, yet?"
asked Constanza, looking into his dark eyes, and
discovering the cloud that shadowed them.
"I am never content with her when you are
by! It is in vain that I have tried to give this
hair the soft ripple of yours! And, oh! that I
could impart to the blank marble the living hues
—the changing gold of the locks—the celestial
blue of the eyes—the rose-tint of the lips! The
statue looks so cold and senseless when you are
before me, that I am in despair !"
" Oh ! Andrea, I am sure that it is perfect! But
since you are dissatisfied with your work I must
sit for you once more. It will be the last time,
for the judges visit the studio to-day, and to-
morrow the statue will be admitted into the
palace."
Before Andrea could reply, Constanza had
hurried with Bettina into the ante-chamber. In a
few moments she reappeard, looking more angelic
than ever, in the spotless white robe, girdled
lightly around her flexible waist, and flowing into
folds that clung to her slight form and revealpd its
undulating outlines. Her long hair enveloped her,
like a golden cloud, With unstudied ease, she at
once threw herself into the attitude of the penitent
Mary, and remained motionless. Andrea contem-
plated her in almost breathless silence, then took
up his chisel and gave a few light touches to the
marble—then drew back, and gazed upon the
living form, glowing with life and beauty, and
upon its inanimate copy. Carried away by an un-
governable emotion, he suddenly flung aside the
chisel, and burst into tears.
Constanza, sprang up and hastened to his side—
but his agitat;on was so vialent that he seemed
unconscious of her presence. With gentle force
she drew away the hands that covered his face,
and gathered up her flowing tresses as though to
wipe his eyes. Well might the mingled archness
and poetry of the action make him smile.
"Your Mary will win the prize, Andrea! lam
sure of it ! "

"Will it win both prizes—this above all ! "
answered Andrea, taking her hand.
"Yes—one now, and the other in time. Per-
haps," she added laughing, " when there are a few
wrinkles hero for you to add to your Mary's brow,
that the likeness may be retained. But see how
the sun is marching up the heavens! Come,
Bettina, it warns us to be on our way."
The attendant and her beloved young mistress
retired again and quickly returned, Constanza
wearing her usual dress.
"Farewell, Andrea, to-morrow morning I will
oome again to learn what the judges have said.
To learn ? " she continued gaily, why I can
prophesy their words—l shall have nothing to
learn, only a sweet confirmation to hear. Do not
shake your head—l am sure of their verdict—fare-
well!

_
The leave-taking between the young lovers was
hardly as warm as might have been expected.
They clasped hands—she with trustful, yet
tremulous timidity—ho with tender reverence.
Such had ever been the reserved character of their
intercourse. _ _

As the door closed the young sculptor turned
again to his Mary. A thousand glannif defects
became suddenly apparent to his excited unagina-
nation—all the features were distorted—the lines
were faulty—.the whole expression was tame—
senseless! He could not endure the sight of his
work, and impetuously drew the crimson curtain,
vowing that he would not throw back its folds
until the judges arrived.
There was no likelihood of their. appearance
before noon—yet he did not dare to absent himself
from the studio even to break his fast. He sat
with his head leaning on his hands, lost in thought,
and, while he mused, the gates of fancy opened to
every fantastic fear that presented itself for ad-
mission.

Hour after hour passed, and now he began to
start at every step that approached his door, his
heart palpitated and his breath became thick—but
the steps passed carelessly on, as though no one
were conscious of his existence. The garish light
began to soften and fade—surely it must be even-
ing! Andrea shuddered at the terrible possibility
that he had been wholly forgotten.
A loud rap on the door put flight to this last tor-
menting fiend. The judges had come. As they
entered Andrea thought they glanced around the
bare apartment with an expression of undisguised
scorn.

Ile faltered out, "You are very welcome—it was
so late, I almost feared--"
One of the judges interrupted him and answered
gruffly-, "Yes, we are late—we have made the
rounds of the studios, and a fatiguing time we
have had of it; this is the last—we must get
through quickly while the light serves."
His tone expressed not merely impatience, but
the conviction that they could meet with no artistic
achievement in that locality which would require
much examination, or give rise to any prolonged
discussion.

Andrea seized the crimson curtain with a con-
vulsive grasp, threw it aside, and turned away,
that he might not see the condemning countenances
of his merciless critics. Large drops of dew
started from his brow; a cold tremor ran through
his frame; his heart sank as with the pressure of
a leaden weight. The door which opened to
admit those stern-visaged old men had let out his
last hope. His only str.iggle now was to bear th

"Oh ! Andrea, has your master-piece been

With almost maniacal vehemence, Andrea re-

"Your disgrace, Constanza!" he added, wildly,

He seized a heavy mallet, and, with a few blows,

to stay his arm—even Bettina interposed, and

moment he stood before the exquisite marble form,

The work of destruction went rapidly on—the
hand that held the box of ointment was smitten—
the white arm fell—the glorious shape was muti-
lated—still the blows were repeated with frantic
force.
Neither Andrea nor the young girl, nor her
attendant had heard the door open. It was not
until a shriek of terror escaped from Bettina, that
they beheld two old men standing upon the thres-
hold, mute spectators of the scene.
One was the judge who had warned Andrea,
the other was the father of Constanza!
The former, fearing to trust the sculptor's de-
cision, had informed his noble friend of the dis-
covery he had made, and hastened with him to
Andrea's studio, at an hour too early for the statue
to have been sent to the palace.
The duke's just indignation melted at the sight
of that heroic deed of self-renunciation. He
recognisedland respected the nobility of spirit that
nerved the young sculptor's heart and arm—the
man he would have spurned an hour before was
transformed into a hero—was raised to an equal.
He strode past `the trembling Constanza, and
laid his hand on Andrea's arm, just as it was lifted
for another blow.
" Enough ! I would contemplate what is left of
this wonderful work, which ley friend so highly
commends."
Andrea's excitement suddenly subsided—his
knees knocked together—a livid hue overspread
his countenance—the lids dropped over his glaring
eyes —he tottered, and would have fallen, if the
pitying judge had not received him in his arms,
and tenderly placed him in a chair.
"Pardon Constanza! visit no wrath upon her,"
Aindrea murmured faintly.
"She is pardoned," answered the Duke, ex-
tending his arms to receive her. The weeping girl
gratefully clung to his bosom, but with her eyes
fixed imploringly upon her half insensible lover.
" Andrea! ' said the Duke, "you have
achieved a greater triumph than if your statue
had obtained the prize; and you have who
a friend whose trust in you, the experience of this
hour proves that you will never betray."
• • • •
The Duke had not misjudged the character of
the gifted sculptor. Not oven his profound pas-
sion for Constanza ever tempted him to return her
father's generous confidence with treachery.
Though he and Constanza often met, it was never
again in secret, and Andrea breathed no word of
love into the maiden's ear. Time tested, and for-
bearance strengthened their affection. Andrea's
powers as a sculptor kept steady pace with his
ambition. In a few years he won renown, and,
with it, a richer guerdon—for the Duke bestowed
upon him the hand of his daughter.
But this dearest triumph was wrought, not by
the fame which crowned his genius, but by the
glorious victory be had gained over himself.

articles.title: OUR MISCELLANY.
articles.text:
OUR MISCELLANY.

ANECDOTE OF FRANKLIN.
A young person ones mentioned to Dr. Franklin
his surprise that the possession of riches should be
attended with undue solicitude, and instanced a
merchant, who, in possession of unbounded wealth,
was as busy, and much more anxious, than the
most industrious clerk in his counting-house. The
doctor, in reply, took an apple from a basket; and
presented it to a child in the room, who could
hardly grasp it in his hand. Ito then gave him a
second, which filled the other; and choosing a
third, remarkable for its size, ho offered that also.
The child, after many ineffectual attempts to hold
the three apples, dropped the last on the carpet,
and burst Into tears. " See," said the doctor,
"there is a little man with more riches than he can
enjoy."

A BILLION.
What a very great sum is a billion! It is a
million of millions. A million seems large enough
—but a million of millions! how long do you
suppose it would take you to count it? A mill
which makes one hundred pins a minute, if kept
to work night and day, would only make fifty-two
millions five hundred and ninety-six thousand
pins a year—and at that rate the mill must work
twenty-thousand years without stopping a single
moment, in order to turn out a billion of pins! It
is beyond our reach to conceive it—and yet when
a billion of years shall have gone, eternity will
seem to have Just begun. How important then is
the question, Whore shall I spend eternity ?"
WAIT A LITTLE LONGER!
Hoot away despair!
Never yield to sorrow;
The blackest sky may wear
A sunny face to-morrow.
LITTLE COURTESIES.
How much of meaning, of refinement, ay, of
Christianity itaolf, there is in those little incidental
attentions and politenesses which go a great way
in making up the beauty of life!
We have known .ri many pooplQ—good

warm-hearted and generous—who were capable of
almost any act of self-sacrifice'and abnegation, who
would never have condescended to raise their hat
to a lady, or offer her a glass of water, before
drinking themselves. This is frequently the fault
of a cross-grained nature, but perhaps most often
the result of early education. Indeed, we always
think a man's manners are the "living epistle
known and read of all men," of his mother's train-
ing. Habitual politeness can only make a mau a
thorough gentleman—a woman a true lady. And
it is most easily acquired in childhood, azid in
one's own household. If a boy be respectful and
courteous to his sisters, he will be so to all women
as long as he lives but if his intercourse with
them be coarse, careless, abrupt, not softened and
refined by a thousand nameless little attentions
and graces, he will be rough, awkward—not ful-
filling always the beautiful injunction of the
apostle, "Be ye courteous to all men." Then,
too, outward refinement influences and softens
the inward character; for it is a law of our being
that "expression intensifies the emotions and feel-
ings." But this work, after all, lies with every
mother in the land—in the world ; and we can only
hope that these hints may influence some to con-
sider it.

HOW TO LOOK YOUNG.
How is it that some men thought to be so old,
still look so young, while others thought young
must still look old F The cause lies very frequently
in themselves. Mr. Rant, once, on being aviced
the reason said—" I never ride when I can walk;
I never wit but one dish at dinner; I never get
drunk. My walking keeps my blood in circulation;
my simple diet prevents indigestion; and never
touching ardent spirits, my 'liver never fears being
eaten up alive." But he forgot to add one of the
greatest causes of lasting youth, "a kind, unen-
vions heart.", Envy can dig as deeply in the
human face as time itself.

HOW WOLVES CAPTURE WILD HORSES.
Whenever wolves associate together for mis-
chief, there is always a numerous train of smaller
ones to follow in the rear, and act as auxiliaries in
the work of destruction. Two large wolves are
sufficient to destroy the most powerful horse, and
seldom more than two ever begin the assault, al-
though there may be a score in the gang. It is
no less curious than amusing, to witness their in-
genious mode of attack. if there is no snow, or
but little on the ground, two wolves approach in
the most playful and caressing manner, lying,
rolling and frisking about, until the too credulous
and unsuspecting victim is completely put of his
guard by curiosity and familiarity. During this
time, the gang, squatting, are looking on at a dis-
tance. After some time spent in this way, the
two assailants separate, when one approaches the
horse's head, the other his tail, with a shyness and
cunning peculiar to themselves. At this stage of
the attack, their frolicsome approaches become very
interesting; the former is mere decoy, the latter
is the real assailant, and keeps his eyes steadily
fixed on the hamstrings or flank of the horse. The
critical moment iathen watched, and the attack is
simultaneous; both wolves spring at their victim
at the same instant—one to the throat, the other
to the flank—and if successful, which they gene-
rally are, the hind one never lets go his hold till
the horse is completely disabled. Instead of
springing forward, or kicking to disengage himself,
the horse turns round and round, without attempt-
ing a defence. The wolf before then springs be-
hind to assist the other. The sinews are then out,
and in half the time I have been describing it, the
horse is on his side; his struggles are fruitless—
the victory is won. At this signal, the lookers-on
close in at a gallop; but the small fry of followers
keep a respecful distance until their superiors are
gorged, and then they take their turn unmolested.

articles.title: BATTLE FIELD.
articles.text:
A BATTLE FIELD.

The grouping of falling men and horses, the
many heaped-up masses of dead moved strangely
by the living maimed among them, showing the
points where the deadly strife had been most
severe; commingling of uniforms of friends and
foes, as both lie scattered on the ground on which
they fell; the groups surrounding this and that
individual sufferer, hearinglhis last words, giving
to him the last drops of water which will ever
moisten his lips upon earth; the stretcher borne
from various points, each carrying some officer or
private soldier, who has now the startling feeling
forced upon him: "It has come to this, and yet
there may be hope of life ;" his excited but over-
worn spirit, half-fainting as it is, yet dreaming a
mixed feverish &cam of the charge in which he
, met his wound, and the thoughts of home that
flashed upon the heart as it seemed to commit that
heart to a moment's oblivion of all else. Then
comes the first dawn of the hope that life may be
spared; the view of honied objects passed, seen
with a dimmed eye; hope of life growing
stronger, but with it now a dread of wino ope-
ration to be undergone; the sound of guns still
heard, begetting a feverish, impatient desire to
know the result of the battle. Again, a partial
waking up at the voice of the surgeon;' he and
his attendants seen as through a mist; the deaf-
ened feelings of utter weakness causing all to
seem as though they spoke in whispers; the
still further rousing of the mind as the cordial
administered begins to take effect; the voice of a
comrade or friend lying close by, himself
wounded, yet speaking to cheer; the operation
borne bravely, and felt the loss as it gives pro-
mise of a life just now seemingly lost to hope ;
through it all fresh news ever arriving from
amidst the din of the strife yet raging; all this
has a life and motion, and spirit in it, which
mocks the real grave horror of the scone.

BRAHMA HEN LAYING SOFT EGGS.—I have A
Brahma pullet batched in April, and commenced

a room where the sun shines in through the win-

light should be deep and not very brilliant.

bottle will appear to glow with great beauty,
