STANDING ARMIES AND THE
WORKING CLASSES.
To the Editor of the BEE•lirvE.
Sr,—The letter which I wrote upon Mr.
Latham's article seems to have engaged the
attention of Mr. Redfearn, who favoured you
with a reply in, your last edition. What his
meaning really is, I think I have made out
after some consideration. He seems to have
got the ider., that myself and those who are not
favourable to our army and navy being dis-
banded at present, are fond of war and opposed
to International Arbitration. In this he is
very much mistaken, for I believe I am as
anxious that war should be abolished as any
of my fellow countrymen.
Mr. Redfearn takes up the question in the
usual manner, grumbling, lamenting, and
sneering at our military and naval institutions.
He says it is not only a pity but a shame that
such a thing as a- standing army should' be
tolerated in Christian England. He might
.mention many other of our institutions
whioh are a sham to a " Christian " country,
but he would probably have to leave the
matter as he leaves this, without suggesting
any reasonable remedy.
He tells us that "rather than we should
permit such a monstrous injustice to continue
in our land he would rather that the sun of
England should set for ever." I must confess,
Mr. Editor, that upon reading this unpatriotic
admission I could not help calling to my mind
the lines of Scott—
Breathe there the man, with soul so dead,
Who never tohimself hath said—
This is my own, my native laud;
If such there breathe, go, mark him well,
For him no minstrel strains shall swell,
High though his titles, proud his name,
Boundless his wealth, as wish can claim.
Despite those titles, power, and pelf,
The wretch concentred all in self,
Living shall forfeit fair renown,
.And doubly dying shall go down
To the vile dust from when he sprung,
Unwept, urthottoured, and unsung.
He has also such a pitiable opinion of the
courage and power of our soldiers and sailors,
that "if Russia or Prussia were to declare
war against us ' he would tremble for the con-
setrences." I sincerely hope that such a
thing may never happen, but if it were to
take place I have an idea that it would not
cause everybody to " tremble " like Mr.
Redfearri.
The substance of my whole letter was con-
tained in the sentence "that our army is a
necessity, a dreadful necessity, a deplorable
necessity, but it is a necessity.' This expres-
sion Mr. Redfearn takes up, and I was in
hopes that he was able to prove that it was
not a necessity, but he runs away from that
question altogether.
He says that my comparing the army to
the police looks "well upon the surface, '
but when examined closely is found to be a
"bugbear.". I imagine from that statement
that he has examined it closely, and dis-
covered "that the police are employed to
bring men to justice, while armies are only
kept similar to men keeping bull-dogs, to let
loose at each other upon the slightest possible
pretext." He has discovered part of the
truth, but not the whole truth. Police are em-
ployed to prevent perpetration:of crime by their
existence, as much as to bring men to justice
after having broken the laws. And as to
armies being compared to bull-dogs Which are
kept for fighting each other, I certainly fail to
see the force of his reasoning.
But coming to the question of "Courts of
Arbitration," allow me to say that I am as
much in favour of them when practical as any
of the readers of the BEE-HIVE. But upon
what ground they would ask us to disband our
forces and render ourselves 'defenceless before
these tribunals are established, I fail to under-
stand. Mr. Redfearn asks if the Alabama
question would not ten years ago have been
the cause of war between two countries.
This is perhaps impossible for us to determine,
but scarely ten months ago the wisest in the
land were in doubt whether peacewould be pre-
served, and the" Court of Arbitration "prove
successful. if it is so difficult to settle matters
between two nations so nearly related and so
highly civilized, how could we be sure that
fighting, demi-civilized. Russians and Turks
would listen to arbitration. I find it difficult
to understand Mr. Redfearn when he says that
" England is a nation who will give justice
and have justice done to her without having
recourse to standing armies." By what
moral power" we could prevail upon other
countries to do us justice, I should very much
like to know. •
In conclusion, I am sorry that Mr. Redfearn
has not had sufficient time since my letter
appeared to give the matter full consideration,
but I should very much like him to "do full
justice to the subject,' and an- grapple with the
question as it really exists.- It is not whether
it is a shame or not for us to have an army,

but how we can safely do without it? whether
we are to abolish our army before "Courts of
Arbitration" are acknowledged and estab-
lished. From my point of view Ido not see
any better way of preserving peace than being
fully prepared for war.
Hoping I have not taken too much of your
valuable space, I am, yours truly,
W. BRUCE.
Heekmondwicke, Oct. 2nd, 1872.

STANDING ORDERS.

1. The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing bona fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
name they may, for the time being, be called.
2. Each delegate shall come provided with a
, oredential signed by the officers of the society or
council he represents, certifying to his appoint-
ment, such credential to be given up to the Secre-
tary, immediately on his arrival at the Con-
gress.
3. The time of meeting shall be as follows :
on the first day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
prompt; on all other days at 9 30 a.m.; adjourn
at 1, re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 5 o'clock
each day.
4. The roll shall be called promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all dele-
gates late or absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.
15. At the opening of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shall
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President.
6. A committee of three shall be elected to
examine the credentials, and report thereon to the
meeting.
7. The delegates shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Congress, preference being given
to a delegate of the town where the Congress is 1
being held.
8. The Congress shall then elect a Secretary, a
like preference being given.
9. The Congress shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, a door-keeper and a messenger.
10. A standing committee of live shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The vice-president
to be the chairman of the committee.
11. After the routine business of election of
officers and committee, the president shall formally
open the Congress witir an address.
12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing aproper despatch of business, with perfect
fairness to all who have been to the trouble to
prepare papers, of which due notice has been
given, shall have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion.
13. The stang committee shall be allowed to

retire at 4 o'clock each day (one hour before
closing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.
14. Each delegate shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10s. towards
the expenses of the Congress • and in ease he
represents more than one society, 108. for every
such society he is delegated to represent. The
names of those who have, and those who have not
paid, to be read over when the roll is called on the
following morning. No person shall be deemed a
member of Congress until his levy is paid.
16. The reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the mover of a resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ten minutes each;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to speak on the question before the chair, but it
shall be at once put to the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an ori-
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but
in case of a dispute, the chairman may order a

division.
18, Two tellers shall be appointed by the Con-
gress, and their ruling shall be final.
19. If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers' of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
21. In the selection of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice hes
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Congress
is being held, shall in no case be allowed to oc-
cupy the time of more than one sitting of the
congress. And it is desirable that these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and embodying'
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No delegate shall leave the room without
the consent of the Vice-President: and delegates
absent one whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
21. A General or Parliamentary Committee of
, nine shall be elected on the last day of each Con-
gress, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors are appointed.
They shall elect from among themselves a
President, Treasurer, and Secretary for the
ensuing year; and they also shall remain
office until they are re-elected, or their successorii
are appointed.
25. All surplus monies after payment of the
expenses of the Congress, ;hall be handed over to
tho Treaanter of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26, The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee shall be (1) to watch all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions of labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Congress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and circumstances may
demand.

27. The officers, under the direction of the
committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or levies, for the purpose of
defrayino• the expenses incurred by such com-
mittee; °but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shall
pay by levy or donation.
28. The Congress having been formally opened
by the President, after the usual routine business
of electing officers and committee, the Parlia-
mentary Committee shall present their report for
the past year, which shell be read by the Parlia-
mentary Secretary, and shall lay it on the table
for discussion by the Congress.
29. The Parliamentary Committee shall a ssist
and co-operate with the local committee of the
town where the next Congress is to be held, for
the purpose of making the arrangements as com-
plete as possible, and preparing the questions to
be discussed, ancitogether to take such joint action
as the business or other special circumstances of
the time may render neeessary or desirable.
30. The Parliamentary Committee, in conjunc-
tion with the local committee, shall be empowered
to invite persons to attend the sittings of the Con-
gress whose presence they may deem advisable
and desirable, such persons to be ellowed to
address the Congress on the invitation of the
Chairman.
